wichtigste: Grazes often arise when falling onto asphalt.
Mainly the top layer of skin is injured.
Especially often affected are the knees and elbows.
A dirty graze is first rinsed with clean water.
On a small graze you stick a plaster.
During healing a scab forms, which you do not pick off.
Knee pads protect when inline skating.

abschnitte.text: A **graze** arises when the skin slides over a rough surface. This often happens when **falling onto asphalt**, gravel or a sports field. This rubs off mainly the **top layer of skin**, the **epidermis**. Beneath it lie many fine nerves, so a graze stings a lot. Children get grazes especially often on **knees and elbows**, because you catch yourself with them when you fall.

Because the wound was in contact with the ground, **dirt and germs** often sit in it. They can cause an **inflammation**. That is why you first **rinse** a dirty graze with **clean water**. Small stones can be removed carefully. Then you disinfect the wound and stick a **plaster** on it. Large or very dirty grazes should be looked at by a doctor.

After a short time a **scab** forms on the wound, a crust of dried blood. It **protects the healing wound** like a natural plaster. Underneath, new skin grows. You should **not pick** the crust, otherwise the wound opens again and heals more slowly. When the skin is finished, the scab falls off by itself.

Anyone who rides inline skates, a skateboard or a scooter protects themselves with **knee pads**, **elbow pads** and wrist guards. A **helmet** also protects the head. Long trousers and sleeves also prevent many grazes. On wet or gravelly ground you go more slowly, because you slip more easily there.

gewusst: Because only the top layer of skin is injured, a graze usually leaves no scar.
Grazes often sting more than small cuts, because a larger area with many nerve endings is exposed.

teile.einleitung: Sterilising means making objects completely free of germs. In hospital this is particularly important for instruments used in operations. It also plays a part in the kitchen and in industry.
wichtigste: **Sterile** means free of germs.
Sterile instruments prevent germs from getting into the wound during an operation.
Sterilising is usually done with great **heat**, often with hot steam.
The machine used for this is called an **autoclave**.
Disinfecting kills many germs, sterilising kills all of them.

abschnitte.text: Tiny **germs** live everywhere around us, for example bacteria, fungi and viruses. Most of them are harmless. But if they get into an open wound, they can cause a dangerous **infection**. An object is **sterile** when not a single living germ is left on it. When **disinfecting**, by contrast, only most of the germs are killed, for example on the hands.

**Heat** is used most often. In hospital, surgical instruments are treated with hot steam under pressure in an **autoclave**. Temperatures of over 120 degrees Celsius are reached. Other methods use hot, dry air, special gases or radiation. Sterile instruments are then tightly packed so that they stay free of germs until the operation.

During an **operation** the team works with sterile instruments, sterile gloves and sterile cloths. They wear masks and caps so that no germs fall into the wound. In the past many people died of infections after operations. In the 19th century doctors such as **Ignaz Semmelweis** and **Joseph Lister** realised how important cleanliness is. Since then operations have become much safer.

The principle also plays a part when **preserving** jam or vegetables. Jars are treated with hot water so that the contents do not go off so quickly. Many **tinned foods** are heated strongly after being sealed and then keep for a very long time. With milk a distinction is made: **pasteurised** milk is heated only briefly and keeps for a few days. More strongly heated **UHT milk** keeps for many weeks unopened.

gewusst: Syringes and cannulas come out of the factory in sterile packaging and are used only once.
Boiling water kills many but not all germs, which is why surgical instruments need higher temperatures.

teile.einleitung: Tarmed was the tariff used in Switzerland to bill outpatient medical services. It set out how much a consultation or an examination costs. From 2026 it was replaced by TARDOC and outpatient flat rates.
wichtigste: Tarmed applied to outpatient medical services.
It was used across Switzerland from 2004.
Every service was rated in tariff points.
The value of a tariff point differed by canton and contract.
Tarmed was a fee-for-service tariff.
Its successors are TARDOC and outpatient flat rates.

abschnitte.titel: One tariff for the whole of Switzerland
abschnitte.text: **Tarmed** governed how doctors' practices and **hospital outpatient departments** billed their outpatient services. Outpatient means that you go home again after the treatment. In 2004 Tarmed replaced the previous **cantonal doctors' tariffs** with one tariff for the whole of Switzerland. Tarmed was a **fee-for-service tariff**. Each individual service, for example five minutes of consultation or an examination, was billed separately.

abschnitte.titel: Tariff points and tariff point value
abschnitte.text: Every service was rated in **tariff points**. To get the price, you multiply the tariff points by the **tariff point value** in francs. An example: 40 tariff points times 0.95 francs makes 38 francs. The number of tariff points was the same across Switzerland, but the tariff point value was agreed regionally. So the same service did not cost the same everywhere.

Doctors' tariffs are negotiated first of all by the **tariff partners**. These are associations of doctors and hospitals on one side and the **insurers** on the other. Only if they cannot agree can the **Federal Council** step in. A different system applies to stays in hospitals for acute somatic care: since 2012, billing has used **SwissDRG** and **case-based flat rates**, that is a fixed amount depending on the diagnosis.

Over time Tarmed came to be seen as **out of date**, because medicine had changed a great deal. After long negotiations the Federal Council approved **TARDOC** and **outpatient flat rates** as successors. They replaced Tarmed from 2026. With flat rates, each individual service is no longer billed. Instead there is a fixed amount for a whole treatment.

gewusst: Every year, many millions of outpatient treatments in Switzerland were billed with Tarmed.
On a doctor's bill under Tarmed you could look up every single service with its tariff number.

teile.einleitung: The forehead is the upper part of the face, between the eyebrows and the hairline. We show feelings with it, and it protects the brain behind it. It plays a part in many sayings.
wichtigste: The forehead lies **above the eyes** and reaches up to the hairline.
Below the forehead grow the **eyebrows**.
The bone under the forehead is called the **frontal bone**.
Frowning often shows that you are thinking or annoyed.
A forehead thermometer can be used to measure a fever.
A headband keeps sweat out of your eyes during sport.
The German saying “jemandem die Stirn bieten” means to stand up to someone bravely.

abschnitte.text: The forehead is the upper part of the face. It reaches from the **eyebrows** to the **hairline**. The eyebrows grow below the forehead and keep sweat and rain out of the eyes. Under the skin lies a flat **forehead muscle**. It raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead. When **frowning**, you often show that you are thinking or not happy.

The skull consists of several bones. At the top front lies the **frontal bone**. It protects the front part of the brain, the **frontal lobe**. This part of the brain helps us, for example, with planning and with controlling movements. In the frontal bone above the eyes there are hollow spaces, the **frontal sinuses**. With a cold they can become inflamed, and then the forehead hurts.

There are **forehead thermometers**, which measure a fever without using the mouth. You hold them against or in front of the forehead and read off the temperature. With a fever people often put a **damp, cool cloth** on the forehead. This feels pleasant and cools the skin a little. During sport people sometimes wear a **headband**. It soaks up sweat so that you can see clearly.

In German, someone who **“offers someone the forehead”** stands up to them bravely and does not simply give in. Someone who “has the forehead” to do something is cheeky or brazen. The forehead also appears in legends: the **unicorn** is a mythical creature that looks like a horse with a horn in the middle of its forehead. In many fairy tales it is seen as noble and hard to catch.

gewusst: Newborn babies do not yet have frontal sinuses, and these only form during childhood.
A head torch is called a “Stirnlampe”, a “forehead lamp”, in German, because you wear it on your forehead with a strap.

teile.einleitung: The oesophagus is a soft muscular tube that connects the throat with the stomach. Every mouthful and every sip of water travels through it. It works with strong muscles and not just with gravity.
wichtigste: The oesophagus is a long, soft **tube** between the throat and the stomach.
In adults it is about **25 centimetres** long.
Waves of muscle push the food downwards.
That is why food reaches the stomach even when you do a handstand.
In the neck the **windpipe** lies directly in front of the oesophagus.
The oesophagus passes through the **diaphragm** to the stomach.
If acidic stomach juice rises back up, **heartburn** results.

abschnitte.text: The oesophagus begins at the back of the throat and ends in the **stomach**. In adults it is about 25 centimetres long, roughly as long as a school ruler. It runs through the neck and the chest, passing behind the heart. Then it goes through an opening in the **diaphragm**. This sheet of muscle separates the chest from the abdomen. Just below it, the oesophagus opens into the stomach.

The wall of the oesophagus is made of **muscles**. When we swallow, they contract one after another, like a wave. This movement is called **peristalsis**. In this way the mouthful is pushed down bit by bit. Because the muscles push actively, food reaches the stomach even during a **handstand**. A mouthful needs only a few seconds, at most about ten, for the whole journey.

In the neck there are two tubes, one behind the other. At the front is the **windpipe** for the air we breathe, behind it the oesophagus for food. When we swallow, the **epiglottis** closes the entrance to the windpipe. This way the food goes down the right tube. If you talk or laugh while eating, something can still get into the windpipe. Then you have to cough hard, because it has “gone down the wrong way”.

At the lower end of the oesophagus a ring of muscle makes sure that the stomach contents stay in the stomach. Sometimes, though, **acidic stomach juice** flows back into the oesophagus. This burns behind the breastbone and is called **heartburn**. It can happen after very fatty, spicy or rich food. Anyone who often has heartburn should have it checked by a doctor.

gewusst: Astronauts can eat in weightlessness because the oesophagus actively pushes the food to the stomach.
The oesophagus is usually collapsed and opens only when a mouthful slides through it.

teile.einleitung: The dead space is the part of the airways in which no gas exchange takes place. The air in it does enter the body, but it does not reach the air sacs of the lungs. That is why it matters for breathing how deeply and how fast you take in air.
wichtigste: The anatomical dead space of an adult amounts to about 150 millilitres.
It includes the nose, throat, windpipe, bronchi and bronchioles.
Air sacs that are ventilated but not supplied with blood make up the alveolar dead space.
Anatomical and alveolar dead space together make up the physiological dead space.
Shallow, fast breathing is not very effective, because a lot of air stays in the dead space.
A very long snorkel increases the dead space.

abschnitte.text: Oxygen enters the blood only in the **alveoli**, the tiny air sacs of the lungs. The routes leading there, that is the **nose**, **throat**, **windpipe**, **bronchi** and **bronchioles**, only pass the air on. They make up the **anatomical dead space**. In an adult this is about **150 millilitres**. This air goes in and out again with every breath without reaching the alveoli.

Sometimes alveoli are ventilated but **not supplied with blood**. Then they too take no part in gas exchange and make up the **alveolar dead space**. This is typical in a **pulmonary embolism**: a clot blocks a pulmonary artery, and the alveoli behind it no longer receive blood. Together, anatomical and alveolar dead space make up the **physiological dead space**. In a healthy person it is almost the same size as the anatomical one.

With the **Bohr dead space equation** you can calculate the dead space. It compares the content of **carbon dioxide** in the exhaled air with that in the air of the alveoli. From this you find out what share of a breath did not take part in gas exchange. The equation goes back to the Danish physiologist Christian Bohr.

The dead space stays the same size with every breath. In a normal breath of about half a litre, most of it reaches the alveoli. With **shallow, fast breathing**, however, the dead space makes up a much larger share, and little fresh air is left for the alveoli. A **long snorkel** is also additional dead space: you breathe in your own CO2-rich air again. That is why snorkels are short.

gewusst: As a rough rule of thumb, the anatomical dead space is about 2 millilitres per kilogram of body weight.
Breathing tubes and masks in medicine also increase the dead space, which is why they are built as short as possible.

teile.einleitung: **Scurvy** is a disease caused by a lack of vitamin C. In the past it mainly affected sailors on long voyages. Today we know that fresh fruit and vegetables give reliable protection.
wichtigste: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C.
In the past it mainly struck sailors on long sea voyages.
A typical sign is bleeding gums.
In 1747 James Lind showed that oranges and lemons help.
James Cook took sauerkraut with him on his voyages.
Vitamin C is sensitive to heat.

abschnitte.text: On **sea voyages** lasting months there used to be no fresh fruit or vegetables. The sailors ate mainly ship's biscuit, salted meat and other food that kept well. After a few weeks many fell ill with **scurvy**. Many even died of it. For a long time nobody knew what caused it.

In scurvy the body lacks **vitamin C** for weeks. It needs this vitamin to build strong **connective tissue**. Without it, blood vessels and tissue become fragile. The **gums bleed**, wounds heal badly and teeth can fall out. With fresh fruit and vegetables, however, scurvy heals quickly.

In 1747 the Scottish ship's doctor **James Lind** carried out a famous experiment. He divided sick sailors into groups and gave each group a different remedy. Only the group with **oranges and lemons** recovered quickly. His experiment is therefore considered one of the first planned comparison trials in medicine. The seafarer **James Cook** later took, among other things, **sauerkraut** with him, which keeps for a long time and still contains enough vitamin C.

There is a lot of vitamin C in **peppers**, **kiwis**, citrus fruit, **cabbage** and berries. Cereals, fat and sugar, on the other hand, contain hardly any. Vitamin C is **sensitive to heat** and is also destroyed by oxygen. It also dissolves into the cooking water. That is why a lot is lost with long cooking, while brief steaming preserves it.

Most animals can make vitamin C themselves. **Humans** cannot, because they lack an enzyme for it. The same goes for the **guinea pig**. That is why guinea pigs need fresh vegetables every day. Anyone who keeps guinea pigs should definitely know this.

gewusst: The chemical word for vitamin C, ascorbic acid, means something like “acid against scurvy”.
English sailors were later given citrus juice regularly and so got the nickname “Limeys”.

teile.einleitung: Extending is one of the most important movements of our body. When we extend a joint, it is straightened, for example the knee when jumping or the elbow when throwing.
wichtigste: When extending, a joint is straightened.
The opposite of extending is bending.
Muscles can only pull, which is why they work in pairs.
The front thigh muscle straightens the knee.
When taking off for a jump, you straighten your legs powerfully.
Many people stretch after waking up.
Downward dog is a well-known stretching exercise from yoga.

abschnitte.text: A muscle can only contract and pull on a bone as it does so. It cannot push. That is why there are muscles on both sides of every joint. In the upper arm the **biceps** bends the elbow, and the **triceps** on the back straightens it again. Such opponents are called **antagonists**. While one muscle works, the other relaxes.

At the front of the thigh lies a very large muscle with four heads, the **quadriceps**. It pulls on the lower leg over the kneecap and so straightens the knee. At the back of the thigh lie the muscles that bend the knee. When climbing stairs, standing up and jumping, the front thigh muscle does a lot of work.

Before a high jump you bend your knees. On **take-off** you straighten your legs powerfully and so push yourself off the ground. When throwing, too, the arm swings forwards and is fully straightened at the end so that the ball flies far. In **gymnastics** gymnasts pay attention to pointed toes and straight knees. This shows a clean posture and earns points.

After sleeping, many people have a good long stretch in bed. This wakes up the muscles and feels good. Many animals such as cats and dogs also stretch after resting. In **yoga** there are many stretching exercises. In **downward dog** the body forms an upside-down V, and the back, arms and legs are stretched. You should stretch slowly and without pain.

gewusst: The quadriceps is one of the largest and most powerful muscles in the body.
Cats also often have a long and thorough stretch after sleeping.

teile.einleitung: Tendons are the strong ropes that connect muscles to bones. Without them a muscle could not move a bone. You can even see some tendons under your skin.
wichtigste: A tendon connects a muscle to a bone.
Tendons consist of strong, tough fibres and are very resistant to tearing.
A tendon cannot contract by itself, only the muscle can.
Tendons look whitish and shiny, muscles are red.
On the back of the hand you see tendons when you spread your fingers.
Too much strain can inflame a tendon.

abschnitte.text: A **tendon** is like a strong rope between muscle and bone. It consists of many strong **fibres** that lie close together. That is why it is tough and hardly stretchable. Tendons look **whitish** and shiny, while muscles are red. They withstand very large pulling forces without tearing.

abschnitte.titel: The muscle pulls, the tendon transmits
abschnitte.text: When a muscle tenses, it becomes shorter and pulls on its tendon. The tendon passes this pull on to the bone, and the bone moves. The tendon itself, however, **cannot contract**. It does not work itself but only passes on the force of the muscle. Muscle, tendon and bone together form a team.

If you spread your fingers, you see tendons stand out under the skin on the **back of the hand**. They run from the muscles in the forearm to the fingers. Many tendons of the hand glide in **tendon sheaths**. These are coverings that lie like a tunnel around the tendon. In them the tendon can glide easily back and forth.

Below the **kneecap** lies a strong tendon. When the doctor taps on it with a small hammer, the muscle at the thigh is briefly stretched. In response it contracts in a flash, and the lower leg shoots forwards. This is called a **reflex**. This is how the doctor checks whether nerves and muscles work well together.

If a tendon is **strained too much** for a long time, it can become inflamed. This happens, for example, with movements that are always the same, such as a lot of typing or one-sided training. The spot then hurts and needs rest until it has recovered. Warming up before sport and breaks help to spare tendons. The largest tendon in the body is the **Achilles tendon** at the heel.

gewusst: The Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel bone and is the strongest tendon in humans.
Tendons have a poorer blood supply than muscles, which is why they heal more slowly.

teile.einleitung: **Sunglasses** protect the eyes from glaring light and from harmful UV rays. They are particularly important in the mountains, in the snow and near water. But not every pair of dark glasses protects well.
wichtigste: Good sunglasses keep out UV rays and soften glaring light.
In the mountains the UV radiation is stronger.
Snow and water reflect a lot of sunlight.
Without protection, snow blindness can develop in the snow.
Even with sunglasses you must never look directly at the sun.
Dark glasses without a UV filter can even do harm.

abschnitte.text: Sunlight contains **UV radiation**, which you cannot see. It can harm the eyes. Good sunglasses keep out these rays. They also soften **dazzling light**, so that you see more comfortably. When buying them, make sure the glasses have **UV protection**, for example with the label UV 400.

In Switzerland sunglasses are particularly important in the **mountains**. The higher you are, the stronger the UV radiation. **Snow** and **water** also reflect a lot of sunlight. The light then reaches the eyes from below as well. When skiing, people often wear **ski goggles**, which fit closely to the face and also protect against wind and snow.

Anyone who spends a long time in the snow without protection can become **snow-blind**. Too much UV light burns the **cornea** of the eye. The eyes then hurt badly, water and are sensitive to light. For a while you see poorly. It usually heals after a few days, but it is very unpleasant.

Behind dark lenses the **pupil** opens so that more light gets into the eye. If there is no UV filter, **more harmful radiation** then gets into the eye than without glasses. That is why cheap dark glasses without UV protection are bad. The colour of the lenses says nothing about the UV protection. The only thing that matters is the built-in filter.

Even with sunglasses you must **never look directly at the sun**. They do not protect enough against direct sunlight. The retina can be **permanently damaged**. To watch a **solar eclipse** you need special **eclipse glasses**. They let through only a tiny part of the light.

gewusst: Centuries ago the Inuit already carved snow goggles out of bone or wood with narrow slits to prevent snow blindness.
Even on cloudy days a large part of the UV radiation gets through the clouds.

teile.einleitung: Social jet lag is the name for the difference between sleep on school or work days and sleep on days off. The body clock often wants to sleep later than the alarm clock and the timetable allow. The name recalls the tiredness after a flight across several time zones.
wichtigste: Social jet lag measures the difference in the **midpoint of sleep** between work days and days off.
It happens when school or work does not fit the body clock.
Teenagers and late chronotypes are particularly strongly affected.
The conflict is usually greatest on Monday morning.
At the weekend many people catch up on accumulated lack of sleep.
Studies link a large social jet lag with a higher risk of being overweight.
Plenty of daylight in the morning can help to move the body clock earlier.

abschnitte.text: Every person has a **body clock** that decides when we are tired and when we are awake. Some people are lively early on, and they are called larks. Others only really wake up late in the evening, and they are called owls. This natural tendency is called a **chronotype**. If owls have to get up early every morning, their body lives against its own rhythm. This conflict is called **social jet lag**, because it is caused by social times such as school and work.

You find the **midpoint of sleep**, that is the moment exactly halfway between falling asleep and waking up. If someone sleeps from 11 pm to 6.30 am on school days, the midpoint of sleep is 2.45 am. If the same person sleeps from 1 am to 10 am on days off, it is 5.30 am. The difference is **2 hours 45 minutes**. That is their social jet lag. The bigger this number, the less everyday life fits the body clock.

**Teenagers** usually have a late chronotype: they only get tired late in the evening. Even so, school starts early in the morning. As a result they often sleep too little during the week and build up a **sleep debt**. At the weekend they then sleep much longer and make up for part of it. In doing so the body clock shifts even later. That is why getting up on **Monday morning** is particularly hard.

Observational studies found that people with a large social jet lag more often had a higher **body mass index**, in other words were more overweight. Mood, concentration and performance can also suffer. **Daylight in the morning** can help, because it sets the body clock earlier. Bright light in the evening, for example from screens, tends to do the opposite. Regular sleep times on every day of the week also make the difference smaller.

gewusst: The term “social jet lag” was coined by the chronobiologist Till Roenneberg from Munich.
Many people have social jet lag every week without ever getting on a plane.

teile.einleitung: The eye catches light, but we only see with the brain. The connection between them is the **optic nerve**. It carries the signals from the retina to the brain.
wichtigste: The optic nerve carries the signals from the eye to the brain.
It contains about a million nerve fibres.
The optic nerve is the second of the twelve cranial nerves.
In the optic chiasm, about half of the fibres change sides.
The exit point in the eye is called the optic disc.
Glaucoma can damage the optic nerve.

abschnitte.titel: From the eye to the brain
abschnitte.text: In the **retina**, sensory cells turn light into electrical signals. Nerve cells of the retina bundle these signals. Their long extensions together form the **optic nerve**. It contains about **a million nerve fibres**. It carries the signals from the eye backwards into the brain, as far as the visual cortex at the back of the head.

Humans have **twelve cranial nerves**, which emerge directly from the brain. They are numbered with Roman numerals. The olfactory nerve is cranial nerve I, the optic nerve **cranial nerve II**. Strictly speaking, the optic nerve is even an advanced part of the brain. That is why it is also wrapped by the meninges.

Behind the eyes, the two optic nerves meet in the **optic chiasm**, in Latin **chiasma opticum**. There about half of the fibres change to the other side. This way each half of the brain gets information from both eyes. This is important for spatial vision. After that the fibres run on as the optic tract to the brain.

abschnitte.titel: The optic disc and the blind spot
abschnitte.text: The place where the optic nerve leaves the eye is called the **optic disc**. It is round and bright. Eye doctors can see it well with the **ophthalmoscope**. At this place there are no sensory cells. That is why the **blind spot** arises there, which we do not notice in everyday life, though.

In **glaucoma**, also called **green star**, fibres of the optic nerve die off little by little. Often too high a pressure in the eye is the cause. Because you do not notice it for a long time, regular check-ups with the eye doctor are important. If the optic nerve of one eye is completely severed, that eye is **blind**. The signals from the retina then no longer reach the brain, and dead fibres do not grow back.

gewusst: The optic nerve is only about as thick as a pencil and yet carries about a million fibres.
Because the optic nerve belongs to the brain, doctors looking at the optic disc can sometimes even see signs of diseases in the head.

teile.einleitung: You can get hurt doing sport, for example through a fall, a collision or overloading. Most sports injuries affect muscles, ligaments, tendons, joints or bones. With good preparation and protective equipment, many of them can be avoided.
wichtigste: A **bruise** is caused by a blow or knock and often leaves a mark.
In a **dislocation** a joint jumps out of its normal position.
When you twist your ankle, the ligaments of the **ankle joint** are often injured.
The **anterior cruciate ligament** in the knee tears particularly often in skiing and football.
A **strain** is an overstretching of muscle fibres without a tear.
A **stress fracture** is caused by many small overloads.
A good warm-up is the best way to prevent injuries.

abschnitte.text: A **bruise** is caused by a blow or knock, for example in a collision in football or ice hockey. Small blood vessels burst under the skin and a **blue mark** forms. In a **dislocation**, also called luxation, the surfaces of a joint lose contact. This happens, for example, at the shoulder. The joint has to be put back by a professional, and you never try it yourself.

Most often you go over on the **outer edge of the foot**. When this happens, the outer ligaments of the ankle joint are overstretched or they tear. In the knee, the **anterior cruciate ligament** stabilises the joint during twisting movements. In falls with a twisted knee, for example when skiing or playing football, it often tears. The **Achilles tendon** connects the calf muscle with the heel bone. It is the strongest tendon in the body, but it can tear under sudden strain.

In a **strain** muscle fibres are overstretched but not torn. If fibres tear, it is called a **torn muscle fibre**. Both often happen in fast sprints without a warm-up. A **stress fracture**, by contrast, is not caused by an accident. If you run too much without enough recovery, the bone gets fine cracks, often in the foot. That is why the body needs breaks when it hurts.

For fresh injuries the **RICE rule** helps: rest, ice, compression, meaning a pressure bandage, and elevation. Cooling and raising the injured part reduce the swelling. Most important of all, though, is prevention. After a good **warm-up**, body and mind are ready for the strain. When inline skating, **wrist guards**, knee and elbow pads and a helmet protect against fractures and grazes.

gewusst: In Switzerland football and skiing are among the sports with the most accidents.
The Achilles tendon is named after the Greek hero Achilles, who is said to have been vulnerable only at his heel.

teile.einleitung: Grief is the feeling we have when we lose a loved person or animal. It is completely natural and shows how important someone was to us. Grief feels a little different for every person.
wichtigste: Grief is a natural reaction to a loss.
At a funeral you say goodbye to someone who has died.
In Switzerland many people wear black at a funeral.
The dead are buried in a cemetery.
Flowers and candles are signs of remembrance.
Talking together about the past can comfort you.

abschnitte.text: Someone who is grieving is sad and has **sorrow**, that is worries and a heavy heart. Grief takes a lot of strength. Many people then feel **tired and heavy**, some cannot sleep well or have no appetite. Besides sadness there is often anger, fear or even moments of joy. All these feelings are normal.

At a **funeral**, family and friends come together to say goodbye. In Switzerland the memorial service is also often called an **“Abdankung”**. Many people wear **black** clothes, because black is the colour of mourning with us. In other countries and cultures this can be different, where people wear white, for example.

The dead are buried in a **cemetery**. You can go there to think of them. Often you lay **flowers** on the grave. A burning **candle** is a sign of remembrance and of hope. After a great disaster, **flags are sometimes flown at half-mast**, that is raised only halfway, as a sign of mourning.

It helps children when they may ask questions and get honest answers. **Talking together about the past** keeps the person alive in the heart and comforts. Some people draw a picture, write a letter or look at photos. If you cannot talk to anyone, you can find help around the clock in Switzerland on the number **147** of Pro Juventute.

gewusst: Grief does not always follow the same course. After weeks or months it can suddenly become stronger again, for example on a birthday.
Many people also grieve deeply when they lose a pet.

teile.einleitung: Swimming is one of the most popular sports and an important skill. Anyone who can swim is safer in the water. In Switzerland, with its many lakes and rivers, this is especially important.
wichtigste: In backstroke you lie on your back.
The butterfly is named after an insect.
In Switzerland the SLRG publishes the well-known bathing rules.
You do not jump into cloudy, unknown water.
You do not run at the poolside, because it is slippery.
An Olympic swimming pool is 50 metres long.
The lifeguard looks after the bathers.

abschnitte.text: There are four well-known swimming strokes. In **breaststroke** you lie on your front and move arms and legs at the same time like a frog. In **front crawl** the arms pull alternately through the water, it is the fastest stroke. In **backstroke** you lie on your back. The **butterfly**, also called the **dolphin**, is named after an insect, because the arms swing forward like wings at the same time.

In Switzerland, the **SLRG**, the Swiss Life Saving Society, publishes the well-known **bathing rules**. One of them reads: **do not jump into cloudy, unknown water**, because there may be stones or shallow spots beneath. Further rules say that you should never swim long distances alone and should always supervise small children in the water within reach. You should also not go into the water on a full or completely empty stomach. The SLRG also trains lifeguards.

At the swimming pool, the **lifeguard** looks after the bathers. At the **poolside you do not run**, because the wet floor is **slippery**. Small children who cannot yet swim wear **armbands**. These never replace supervision by adults, though. Many children learn to swim in school swimming or in a swimming course.

**Swimming** has been Olympic since the first modern Olympic Games in 1896. An **Olympic swimming pool** is **50 metres** long. There are competitions in all swimming strokes and over different distances. Swimming trains almost all muscles and is easy on the joints, because the water carries the body. That is why it is a healthy sport for people of any age.

gewusst: An Olympic pool holds several million litres of water.
In many Swiss cities, hundreds of people swim in summer in rivers such as the Rhine or the Aare.

teile.einleitung: **Sepsis** is a life-threatening emergency. The body reacts so violently and wrongly to an infection that organs are damaged. Quick treatment can save lives.
wichtigste: Sepsis is a life-threatening failure of organ function caused by a misdirected response to an infection.
In everyday language it is often called blood poisoning, but this term is inaccurate.
The qSOFA score helps to recognise sepsis early.
In septic shock the circulation needs medicines despite drips.
In septic shock, antibiotics should be given within one hour.
World Sepsis Day is on 13 September.

abschnitte.text: Normally the immune system fights an infection in a targeted way. In **sepsis** this defence gets out of control and harms the body itself. Since the **Sepsis-3** definition of 2016, this misdirected reaction has been at the centre. It can make organs such as the **kidneys**, the **lungs** or the circulation fail. In everyday language people often say **blood poisoning**, although there is no poison in the strict sense.

Outside the intensive care unit, the **qSOFA score** helps to recognise sepsis. It checks three simple signs. These are a breathing rate of 22 or more per minute, an altered **level of consciousness** and a systolic blood pressure of **100 mmHg** or less. If two signs apply, the risk is increased. In the blood, doctors also often measure **lactate**, which rises when tissues lack oxygen.

The most serious form is **septic shock**. Here the blood pressure drops so much that drips alone are not enough. Medicines that support the circulation, called **vasopressors**, are also needed. The death rate is then particularly high. That is why septic shock is treated in the intensive care unit.

If septic shock is suspected, guidelines say **antibiotics should be given within one hour**. With every hour of delay the risk rises considerably. If possible, **blood cultures** are taken beforehand. In them the germs can be grown and tested for resistance. After antibiotics have been given, they often no longer grow.

A large study in the medical journal **“The Lancet”** estimated around 49 million cases of sepsis worldwide for the year 2017. There were about **11 million deaths**. That was around a fifth of all deaths in the world. Even so, many people hardly know the disease. **World Sepsis Day** on 13 September is meant to draw attention to it.

gewusst: Sepsis can develop from quite everyday infections, for example from pneumonia or a urinary tract infection.
Vaccinations, for example against flu or pneumococci, can also help to prevent cases of sepsis.

teile.einleitung: The stirrup is the smallest bone in the human body. It sits deep inside the ear and helps us to hear. It got its name because it looks just like a stirrup on a horse's saddle.
wichtigste: The stirrup is the **smallest bone** in the human body.
It measures only about 3 millimetres and weighs a few milligrams.
Together with the **hammer** and the **anvil**, it is one of the ossicles.
The hammer is attached to the **eardrum**.
The ossicles pass on vibrations, which is how we can hear.
Attached to the stirrup is the **stapedius muscle**, the smallest muscle in the human body.
Every person has two stirrups, one in each ear.

abschnitte.text: The stirrup measures only about **3 millimetres**. It fits easily on a fingertip and weighs only a few milligrams, much less than a grain of rice. No other bone in the body is smaller. It is named after the foot holder used in riding: a stirrup hangs from the saddle and holds the rider's foot. The bone in the ear looks exactly like it. Its technical name is **stapes**.

In the **middle ear**, behind the eardrum, there are three tiny bones: the **hammer**, the **anvil** and the **stirrup**. Their names recall tools and objects from earlier times. The hammer is connected to the **eardrum**. The anvil lies in the middle. The stirrup sits at the end of the chain. Its footplate fits into a small opening to the inner ear, the **oval window**.

Sound makes the eardrum vibrate. When the eardrum vibrates, the hammer moves too. It passes the vibrations on to the anvil, and the anvil passes them on to the stirrup. The stirrup pushes them through the oval window into the fluid-filled **inner ear**. There sensory cells turn the vibrations into signals for the brain. The ossicles amplify the vibrations so that they arrive well in the inner ear.

Attached to the stirrup is the **stapedius muscle**. It is the smallest muscle in the human body. With very loud noises it contracts and makes the chain of ossicles stiffer. This lets less sound into the inner ear, and the ear is protected a little. But this protection is not enough against very loud bangs, which is why people wear **ear protection** in noisy places.

gewusst: The ossicles are already almost their final size at birth.
The hammer, anvil and stirrup together would easily fit on a small coin.

teile.einleitung: Many hormones cannot get into a cell. They deliver their message on the outside, and a second messenger substance inside the cell carries it on. This inner messenger is called a **second messenger**.
wichtigste: A second messenger carries a signal from the cell membrane into the cell interior.
The best-known second messenger is **cAMP** (cyclic adenosine monophosphate).
The enzyme adenylate cyclase makes cAMP from ATP.
A G protein links the hormone receptor with adenylate cyclase.
cAMP switches on protein kinase A.
Another second messenger is IP3, which releases calcium in the cell.
Signal cascades amplify a weak signal very strongly.

abschnitte.text: Peptide hormones such as **glucagon**, and adrenaline too, are water-soluble. The cell membrane, however, consists of a fat-like double layer through which such substances cannot pass. That is why the hormone binds on the outside to a **receptor**, a kind of receiving antenna. The receptor then passes the message on inwards. There a small molecule, the second messenger, takes over the distribution of the signal.

If a hormone binds to a **G protein-coupled receptor**, a G protein is activated inside the cell. It switches on the enzyme **adenylate cyclase**. Adenylate cyclase converts ATP, the cell’s energy carrier, into cAMP. cAMP binds to **protein kinase A** and releases its active parts. These attach phosphate groups to other proteins and so change their work.

Besides cAMP there are other second messengers. **IP3** (inositol trisphosphate) arises from a building block of the cell membrane. It travels to the **endoplasmic reticulum**, a store inside the cell. There it opens channels, and calcium streams into the cell plasma. The calcium then triggers various reactions, for example the contraction of muscle cells.

A single hormone molecule activates many enzyme molecules. Each of these enzymes in turn makes many cAMP molecules. In this way a **signal cascade** arises, which amplifies the signal step by step. From a tiny stimulus comes a large response of the cell. So that the signal also ends again, enzymes called **phosphodiesterases** break down cAMP.

The American **Earl W. Sutherland** found out that hormones such as adrenaline mediate their effect through cAMP. For this discovery he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1971. Later it turned out that caffeine too can inhibit the phosphodiesterases. Then cAMP lasts longer. At the amounts in coffee, though, caffeine acts mainly by blocking adenosine receptors.

gewusst: A single hormone molecule can trigger, through the cascade, the making of very many cAMP molecules.
The same cAMP can have quite different effects in different cells, depending on which proteins are present there.

teile.einleitung: The sympathetic nervous system is part of the autonomic nervous system. In times of stress and danger it prepares the body for action, without our controlling it consciously.
wichtigste: The sympathetic nervous system belongs to the autonomic nervous system.
It is especially active in times of stress and danger.
It speeds up the heartbeat and widens the pupils.
It widens the airways and slows down digestion.
The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline in the process.
The sympathetic trunk runs along both sides of the spine.

abschnitte.text: The **autonomic nervous system** controls the organs without our will, for example the heart, breathing and digestion. It consists of the **sympathetic nervous system**, the **parasympathetic nervous system** and the enteric nervous system of the gut. The sympathetic and parasympathetic systems mostly work as opposites. The sympathetic system is the accelerator, the parasympathetic system the brake for rest and recovery.

In times of stress and danger, the sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for **fight or flight**. It raises the **heart rate** and **blood pressure** so that the muscles get more blood. It widens the **airways** so that more air flows into the lungs. The **pupils** become wider so that more light enters the eye.

In a dangerous situation, digesting is not important. So the sympathetic nervous system **slows down** the activity of the stomach and gut. The flow of saliva also decreases, which is why your mouth goes dry when you are excited. The energy goes instead to the muscles, heart and brain.

On both sides of the spine runs a chain of nerve knots, the **sympathetic trunk**. There many sympathetic nerve fibres are switched over before they travel on to the organs. At the nerve endings the messenger substance **noradrenaline** is at work. In addition, the **adrenal medulla** releases **adrenaline** into the blood. It strengthens the effects of the sympathetic nervous system throughout the body.

gewusst: The sweat glands are also controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, which is why you sweat when you are excited.
The name comes from Greek and means roughly “feeling with”.

teile.einleitung: Sebaceous glands are small glands in the skin. They make sebum, a mixture of fats that keeps skin and hair supple and protects the skin.
wichtigste: Sebaceous glands make skin oil, called sebum.
Most of them open into the hair follicle.
There are no sebaceous glands on the palms of the hands or the soles of the feet.
There are especially many on the face, chest and back.
Sebaceous glands work holocrine: whole cells break down into sebum.
The Meibomian glands on the edge of the eyelid are special sebaceous glands.

abschnitte.text: **Sebum** is a mixture of different fats. Together with sweat it forms a thin **protective film** on the skin. This film keeps the skin supple, protects it from **drying out** and holds back many germs. Sebum also makes the hair soft and shiny.

Most sebaceous glands open into the **hair follicle**, the sheath around the hair. From there the sebum reaches the surface of the skin. The sebaceous glands of the scalp give off sebum constantly. It spreads along the hairs. That is why hair gets **greasy** if you do not wash it for a long time.

Especially many sebaceous glands sit on the **face**, above all in the so-called **T-zone** of forehead, nose and chin, and on the **chest**, the **back** and the scalp. There the skin gets shiny more quickly. On the **palms of the hands** and **soles of the feet**, by contrast, there are no hairs and no sebaceous glands either. In teenagers the glands often produce a lot of sebum, which can lead to spots.

Sebaceous glands work **holocrine**. This means that the gland cells fill up with fat, die and break down. Their whole contents become sebum. New cells grow back all the time. A special form is the **Meibomian glands** on the edge of the eyelids. They release fat into the tear film so that the tear fluid on the eye does not evaporate too quickly.

gewusst: On each eyelid, several dozen Meibomian glands sit side by side.
The word holocrine comes from Greek and means roughly “secreting entirely”.

teile.einleitung: Thermogenesis means heat production. Our body constantly produces heat so that it can keep a temperature of about 37 degrees. This heat arises when we digest food, when we move and, in the cold, also in special ways.
wichtigste: Processing food costs about 10 per cent of the daily energy turnover on a mixed diet.
Protein needs the most energy to be processed, fat the least.
In the cold, muscle shivering quickly produces extra heat.
Non-shivering thermogenesis is especially important in newborns.
Thyroid hormones raise the basal metabolic rate and heat production.
The hypothalamus in the brain controls body temperature.

abschnitte.text: When you eat, you use energy for the digestion, absorption and processing of nutrients. This is called **diet-induced thermogenesis**. On a mixed diet it is about **10 per cent** of total turnover. With **protein**, around 20 to 30 per cent of the energy taken in is needed for processing, and with fat the share is smallest. That is why you sometimes feel warm after a big meal.

When we are cold, we start to shiver. In **cold shivering** the muscles contract quickly and in a disorderly way. They do no work in the process, and the energy becomes almost entirely **heat**. There is also **non-shivering thermogenesis**. Here energy in the metabolism is released directly as heat, mainly in **brown fat tissue**. Babies have especially much of it.

Every movement produces heat, because muscles convert only part of the energy into force. That is why we get hot when we do sport. Movement in everyday life counts too: walking, standing, climbing stairs or fidgeting. Experts call this **NEAT**, short for “Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis”. This share differs very much from person to person.

The temperature centre lies in the **hypothalamus**, a small part of the brain. It compares the measured temperature with the set value and, when needed, starts heat production or cooling by sweating. The **thyroid hormones** thyroxine and triiodothyronine raise the activity of many cells. In an overactive thyroid, people often sweat and hardly ever feel cold.

gewusst: The substance 2,4-dinitrophenol used to be sold as a slimming aid. It is life-threatening, because the energy is released as heat instead of as ATP and the body can overheat.
Even in shivering, so much heat is released that the body's energy use rises clearly.

teile.einleitung: Tinnitus is a noise in the ear that has no outside source of sound. People with it hear, for example, a whistling, rushing or humming. For some it is there only briefly, while for others it stays with them for a long time.
wichtigste: Tinnitus is a noise in the ear without a sound source outside.
The word comes from the Latin “tinnire”, meaning to ring.
Tinnitus is a symptom with various causes, not an illness of its own.
In teenagers, music that is too loud is a common cause.
From about three months' duration it is called chronic tinnitus.
Ear protection and distance from the speakers protect you at concerts.

abschnitte.text: With **tinnitus** you hear a whistling, rushing, droning or humming, although no matching sound comes from outside. The word comes from the Latin “tinnire”, which means **to ring**. Almost all ear noises are **subjective**: only the person affected hears them, and they arise in the hearing pathway. Rarely there is an **objective tinnitus**, which others can also measure, for example an audible rushing of blood.

Tinnitus is a **symptom**, that is, a sign of illness. It can appear after loud **noise**, in **sudden hearing loss** or with **stress**. In teenagers, **music that is too loud** is a common cause, for example in headphones or at concerts. Noise can damage the fine **hair cells** in the inner ear. A whistling after a concert is a warning sign.

At a loud concert it is best to protect yourself with **ear protection** and **distance from the speakers**. Ear protection lowers the sound level in the ear, and with every metre of distance it becomes quieter. With headphones it helps to keep the volume low and to take breaks. In Switzerland there are legal rules on volume for events.

A tinnitus that lasts longer than about **three months** counts as **chronic**, and before that it is called acute tinnitus. Many people with it notice it especially strongly in **quiet surroundings**, for example when falling asleep, because other noises then do not cover it. In **cognitive behavioural therapy** you learn to pay less attention to the noise. In this way the brain often gets used to it.

gewusst: Many people hear a faint ear noise after a while in a completely quiet room.
A quiet background noise, such as a fan, can help you notice the tinnitus less when falling asleep.

teile.einleitung: The radius is one of the two bones in the forearm. It lies on the thumb side and turns around the ulna when we turn our hand. In German it is called “Speiche”, which means the spoke of a wheel.
wichtigste: The radius lies on the **thumb side** of the forearm.
Its Latin name is **radius**.
It turns around the ulna, which lets you turn your hand.
At the wrist it forms most of the joint with the carpal bones.
Above the radius at the wrist you can feel your **pulse**.
A broken radius at the wrist is one of the most common fractures.

abschnitte.text: The forearm has two bones: the **ulna** on the little finger side and the **radius** on the thumb side. The radius runs from the elbow to the wrist. At the top, at the elbow, it has a small, round **head of the radius**, which is covered with cartilage. It turns inside a ring-shaped ligament. Further down the radius becomes wider and carries a joint surface for the **carpal bones**. The ulna takes part there only through a disc of cartilage.

When you turn your hand, the radius turns around the ulna. When the palm faces upwards, the two bones lie parallel next to each other. This movement is called **supination**. A way to remember it: with supination you can carry a bowl of soup. When the palm faces downwards, the radius crosses over the ulna. This movement is called **pronation**. Without this turning we could not turn a key in a lock.

The tendon of the **biceps**, the two-headed muscle of the upper arm, is attached to a bump on the radius. When it contracts, the arm bends at the elbow. The biceps also helps with supination. On the thumb side of the wrist an **artery** lies directly over the radius. If you press it gently against the bone, you can feel the **pulse**. That is why it is often measured exactly there.

Anyone who falls often catches themselves with an outstretched hand. When this happens, the radius often breaks just above the wrist. This **broken radius** is one of the most common fractures in humans. Pain, swelling and sometimes a crooked wrist are typical. Depending on the break, the arm is kept still in a **plaster cast** or operated on. When inline skating, wrist guards protect against injuries like this.

gewusst: The Latin word radius means the spoke of a wheel or a ray, which is also where the radius of a circle gets its name.
In pronation the radius and ulna lie crossed over each other, and in supination they lie next to each other again.

teile.einleitung: Surprise is a feeling that arises when something unexpected happens. It comes suddenly and usually lasts only a short time. Afterwards another feeling often follows, for example joy or fear.
wichtigste: A surprise arises when something unexpected happens.
It usually lasts only a short time.
In a surprise the mouth often opens.
A typical exclamation is “Oh!”.
A sudden, unpleasant surprise is called a fright.

abschnitte.text: You can often recognise surprise by the face. The **eyebrows** go up, and the eyes become wide. The lower jaw drops slightly, and the **mouth opens** into an “oh”. Many people then also call out “Oh!” or “Wow!”. That is why people say “my **jaw dropped**” when they are very surprised.

A surprise is over quickly, often after a few seconds. Afterwards you realise what has actually happened. Then usually another feeling follows. A nice surprise makes you **happy**. A spooky surprise makes you **afraid**. A sudden, unpleasant surprise, such as a loud bang behind your back, is called a **fright**.

Many people like to surprise others. At a **surprise party**, everyone secretly prepares a celebration, and the person being celebrated knows nothing about it beforehand. An unexpected present or a letter from a friend can also be a nice surprise. Someone who is very amazed at something new is **astonished**. Astonishment helps us to discover and learn new things.

gewusst: Researchers often count surprise among the basic feelings that people all over the world show in a similar way.
The face shows surprise so quickly that you can hardly prevent it.

teile.einleitung: The subcutaneous tissue is the lowest layer of the skin. It consists mainly of fatty tissue and loose connective tissue. It warms, cushions and stores energy for the body.
wichtigste: The subcutaneous tissue is the lowest layer of the skin.
It consists mainly of fatty tissue.
The fat protects against cold and stores energy.
Fat cells are called adipocytes in technical language.
At the heel the fat pad acts like a shock absorber.
Pacinian corpuscles in the subcutaneous tissue feel vibrations.

abschnitte.text: The skin consists of three layers. At the very top lies the **epidermis**, below it the **dermis** and at the bottom the **subcutaneous tissue**, called the **subcutis** in technical language. The subcutaneous tissue lies between the dermis and the muscle sheaths below. It connects the skin with the muscles and the bone membrane. Because it is loosely built, the skin can be moved about in many places.

The subcutaneous tissue consists mainly of **fatty tissue**. The fat cells are called **adipocytes**. They lie together in small lobules and store fat in large droplets. The **subcutaneous fat** acts like an insulating layer against cold. It is also an **energy store**: if the body needs more energy than it gets from food, it can draw on this reserve.

In some places the subcutaneous tissue is an important **cushion**. At the **heel** the fat pad is especially thick. It acts like a **shock absorber** with every step. Deep in the subcutaneous tissue also lie the **Pacinian corpuscles**. These sensory corpuscles react especially to **vibrations**, for example when the phone buzzes in your trouser pocket.

Some medicines are injected into the subcutaneous tissue. This is called a **subcutaneous injection**, from “sub” for under and “cutis” for skin. The medicine reaches the fatty tissue and from there is slowly taken up into the blood. This is how many people with **diabetes**, for example, inject their **insulin**. Some vaccinations are also given this way.

Many animals in cold regions have an especially thick subcutaneous layer. **Whales** and **seals** have a thick layer of blubber. This layer keeps them warm in the ice-cold sea water. It also serves as a reserve when the animals eat little for a long time. Polar bears and penguins also protect themselves with fat under the skin.

gewusst: In large whales the layer of blubber can be several dozen centimetres thick.
The subcutaneous tissue is not equally thick everywhere: on the eyelids the fat pad is almost entirely missing.

teile.einleitung: The University Children's Hospital Zurich is one of the largest children's hospitals in Switzerland. Many people simply call it the “Kispi”. There, children and teenagers are treated for minor and for very serious illnesses.
wichtigste: The Children's Hospital Zurich is called the “Kispi” for short.
It is one of the largest children's hospitals in Switzerland.
It treats children and teenagers.
As a university hospital it works together with the University of Zurich.
It is run by a private foundation.

abschnitte.text: At the **Kispi** work doctors, nurses and many other professionals who know especially much about **children and teenagers**. Children are not small adults: their bodies are still growing, and many illnesses take a different course. That is why children's hospitals of their own are needed. At the Kispi, children are treated for emergencies, for rare illnesses and also after serious accidents.

The children's hospital is a **university hospital**. It works closely with the **University of Zurich**. Young doctors learn there how to treat children. A great deal of **research** is also done, so that children's illnesses can be better understood and cured. The Kispi is run by a private foundation, the **Eleonorenstiftung**.

The Children's Hospital Zurich has existed since the 19th century. For a long time it stood in the Hottingen district. At the end of **2024** it moved into a large **new building** in Zurich-Lengg. The new building was designed by the Basel architects **Herzog & de Meuron**. It has a lot of wood and light and is meant to feel friendly for children and their families.

gewusst: Children in hospital often get visits from hospital clowns, who make them laugh and distract them.

teile.einleitung: Thermoregulation means that the body controls its own temperature and keeps it at about 37 degrees Celsius. Whether you are playing in the snow or running in the summer heat, your body makes sure that it does not get too cold or too warm inside. A red face when running or goosebumps in winter are visible signs of this.
wichtigste: The human body keeps its core temperature at about 37 degrees Celsius.
The temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus in the brain.
When you run you go red, because more blood flows to the skin to give off heat.
Sweating cools the body through evaporation.
In the cold we shiver to produce heat.
Humans, mammals and birds are warm-blooded.
A fever is a deliberate rise in body temperature.

abschnitte.text: **Thermoregulation** means regulating heat. The body constantly measures its temperature and balances out deviations. The temperature inside the body, the **core temperature**, is about 37 degrees Celsius in humans. The skin, hands and feet, by contrast, may be clearly cooler. Even a few degrees of deviation inside the body can become dangerous.

The control centre lies in the **hypothalamus**, a small part of the diencephalon. It receives reports from temperature sensors in the skin and in the blood. Like the thermostat of a heating system, it compares the values with the set value. If it is too warm, it switches on cooling. If it is too cold, it makes sure there is more warmth.

When you run, your muscles produce a lot of heat. The blood vessels in the skin **widen**, and more blood flows to the skin to give off heat, which is why your face goes red. At the same time the sweat glands produce **sweat**. When it evaporates on the skin, it draws heat out of the body. That is why it is important to drink a lot in the heat.

In the cold the blood vessels of the skin **narrow** so that less heat is lost, and the skin turns pale. The muscles start to tremble, and this **cold shivering** produces heat. Goosebumps are also a reaction to cold, which in animals with thick fur makes the fur stand up. We also look for warm places and put on warm clothes. Babies additionally have brown fat tissue, which produces heat directly.

Humans, mammals and birds are **warm-blooded**, and they keep their temperature almost always constant. Lizards, snakes, fish and insects, by contrast, are **cold-blooded**. Their temperature depends on their surroundings, which is why lizards bask on warm stones in the morning. Marmots in the Alps greatly lower their body temperature during hibernation. This saves energy over many months.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature inside the body, about 37 degrees in humans.
The part of the brain that, among other things, controls body temperature.
Living things that keep their body temperature constant by themselves.
Animals whose temperature adapts to their surroundings.

gewusst: Dogs can hardly sweat and cool down mainly by panting.
Elephants use their big ears like radiators, through which a lot of blood flows.
Body temperature varies slightly over the day and is lowest in the early morning.

teile.einleitung: A hospital is a place where sick and injured people are examined, treated and cared for. In Switzerland people usually say “Spital”, in Germany rather “Krankenhaus”. Many specialists work together there around the clock.
wichtigste: Someone who is treated in hospital is called a **patient**.
A **name band** on the wrist prevents mix-ups.
At the entrance you disinfect your hands to protect sick people from germs.
Many hospitals have fixed **visiting hours**.
The **X-ray machine** is used to take pictures of the bones.
The university hospital in Bern is called the **Inselspital**.
Wide doors make sure that beds fit through.

abschnitte.text: In a hospital doctors, nurses, therapists and many other specialists work. Anyone who has to stay for several days gets a bed in a **patient's room**, often together with other sick people. The word **patient** comes from Latin and has to do with suffering and patience. The word Spital comes from the Latin hospitalis, meaning hospitable. In the past hospitals were often lodgings for the poor, the sick and travellers.

At the entrance there is usually a dispenser with **disinfectant**. It kills germs on the hands and so protects the sick people. Each patient is often given a **name band** around the wrist. It shows their name and other details so that nobody gets mixed up. Many doors are particularly **wide**, because sick people are often pushed in their bed from one room to another.

A hospital has many machines for examinations. The **X-ray machine** is used to take pictures of the bones. X-rays pass through the skin but not so easily through bone, which is why bones show up on the picture. The rays were discovered by Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen in 1895. There is also, for example, ultrasound, a laboratory for blood samples and operating theatres. In the **accident and emergency department** people who need help immediately are treated.

Switzerland has five **university hospitals**: in Zurich, Bern, Basel, Lausanne and Geneva. There doctors are also trained and new treatments are researched. The university hospital in Bern is called the **Inselspital**, and many people simply call it “die Insel”, meaning “the island”. There are also cantonal hospitals, regional hospitals and children's hospitals. The costs are paid largely by **health insurance** and the cantons.

Many hospitals have fixed **visiting hours**. This way the patients also have enough time to rest. Visitors are quiet and show consideration for other people in the room. Anyone who has a cold themselves should wait until they are well again before visiting. A card or a picture often brings a lot of joy.

gewusst: The Inselspital in Bern was founded in the 14th century and is one of the oldest hospitals in Switzerland.
In a large hospital people work day and night, even at Christmas and on Sundays.

teile.einleitung: A stent is a small support for a blood vessel, usually a fine tube made of metal mesh. It is placed in a narrowed blood vessel and holds it open. This allows blood to flow freely again, for example to the heart muscle.
wichtigste: A stent holds a narrowed blood vessel open from the inside.
It is inserted through a **catheter**, today often through the artery at the wrist.
A balloon-expandable stent is opened out with an inflated **balloon**.
In 1977 in Zurich **Andreas Grüntzig** carried out the first balloon dilation of a coronary artery.
Drug-coated stents prevent the vessel from growing closed again.
Two platelet inhibitors are meant to prevent a blood clot in the stent.
The name goes back to the English dentist **Charles Stent**.

abschnitte.text: Blood vessels can become narrowed by deposits over the course of a lifetime. If this affects the **coronary vessels**, also called coronary arteries, the heart muscle gets too little blood. A stent supports the vessel from the inside and holds it open. Stents are also used for narrowings of the **carotid artery** and the arteries of the legs and kidneys. Everywhere the aim is to restore the blood flow.

The doctor punctures an artery, today often the **radial artery** at the wrist, otherwise the artery in the groin. The stent is brought to the narrow point through a thin **catheter**. It sits folded up on a **balloon catheter**. When the balloon is filled under pressure, the stent expands and presses itself against the wall of the vessel. Afterwards the balloon is deflated and pulled out, and the stent stays.

In **1977**, at the University Hospital Zurich, **Andreas Grüntzig** widened a narrowed coronary artery with a balloon catheter for the first time. This balloon dilation is considered the beginning of **interventional cardiology**, that is the treatment of the heart with catheters instead of major operations. Later came stents, which hold the vessel open after it has been widened. The name stent goes back to the English dentist **Charles Stent**, who developed a material for taking impressions in the 19th century.

After the stent is put in, the vessel can grow closed again, and this is called **restenosis**. **Drug-coated stents** slowly release active substances that slow down cell division in the wall of the vessel. Blood platelets can also gather on the foreign material and form a clot. That is why patients usually receive two **platelet inhibitors**, for example acetylsalicylic acid and clopidogrel. **Bioresorbable** stents are made of materials that break down, such as lactic acid polymers or magnesium, and dissolve over time.

gewusst: A stent for a coronary vessel, when folded up, is only a little thicker than a pencil lead.
Many patients are awake while a stent is put in and receive only a local anaesthetic.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss vaccination schedule says which vaccinations are recommended at which age. It is published by the Federal Office of Public Health together with an expert commission and revised regularly. In Switzerland, vaccinations are in principle voluntary.
wichtigste: In Switzerland there is no general compulsory vaccination, vaccinations are in principle voluntary.
Basic vaccinations are recommended for everyone to protect personal and public health.
Supplementary vaccinations offer individual protection but do not count as basic for everyone.
Infants get the six-in-one vaccination at 2, 4 and 12 months.
The two MMR vaccinations are recommended at 9 and 12 months.
If the hepatitis B vaccination is missing, it is caught up between 11 and 15 years.
From 65 years, the yearly flu vaccination is recommended for everyone.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss vaccination schedule** is a list of recommendations. It is drawn up by the **Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH)** together with the **Federal Commission for Vaccination**. It says which diseases you should be vaccinated against and at what age. Doctors follow it. Because research goes on, the schedule is adjusted regularly.

The schedule distinguishes several groups. **Basic vaccinations** are recommended for everyone, because they protect one’s own health and that of the whole population. **Supplementary vaccinations** offer individual protection but do not count as basic for everyone. In addition there are vaccinations for **risk groups**, that is, for people who are especially at risk. One example: from **65 years**, the yearly **flu vaccination** is recommended for everyone.

Even infants are vaccinated against several diseases at the same time. The **six-in-one vaccination** protects against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, **polio**, **Haemophilus influenzae type b** and **hepatitis B**. It is given at **2, 4 and 12 months**. Against measles, mumps and rubella there is the **MMR vaccination**, recommended at **9 and 12 months**. Several doses are needed so that the protection lasts a long time.

If a vaccination was missed, you can usually **catch it up**. The vaccination against **hepatitis B**, for example, is recommended **between 11 and 15 years** if it was not given in infancy. In adolescence and adulthood too, some **booster vaccinations** are needed, for example against tetanus. In the **vaccination record**, every vaccination is entered, so you can see at any time what is still missing.

In Switzerland there is **no general compulsory vaccination**. Vaccinations are in principle **voluntary**, and each person, or for children the parents, decides for themselves. The experts recommend the basic vaccinations because they protect against severe diseases. When many people are vaccinated, some diseases can hardly spread any more. This also benefits people who cannot be vaccinated themselves.

gewusst: Thanks to vaccinations, polio has been regarded as eradicated in Europe since 2002.
The vaccination record also exists in electronic form.

teile.einleitung: The heart beats without us having to think about it. The rhythm is set by the **sinus node**, a small group of special heart muscle cells. That is why it is also called the heart's natural pacemaker.
wichtigste: The sinus node lies in the wall of the right atrium.
Every normal heartbeat starts there.
The AV node passes the impulse on to the ventricles with a delay.
The bundle of His carries the impulse on into the ventricles.
The vagus nerve slows the heartbeat down.
Below 60 beats per minute is called bradycardia, over 100 at rest tachycardia.

abschnitte.text: The **sinus node** is a small cluster of special heart muscle cells in the wall of the **right atrium**. These cells produce electrical impulses by themselves. Each impulse triggers a **heartbeat**. That is why the heart beats even without a command from the brain. At rest, the sinus node sets a rate of about 60 to 80 beats per minute in adults.

From the sinus node the impulse spreads across the atria, and they contract. Then it reaches the **AV node** between the atria and the ventricles. It **slows down** the impulse briefly so that the ventricles can first fill with blood. After that the **bundle of His** carries the impulse into the wall between the ventricles. Through fine fibres it spreads into all the muscle of the ventricles.

The sinus node adjusts the rhythm. During exertion or excitement the heart beats faster. The **vagus nerve**, on the other hand, slows the sinus node down, for example during sleep. It belongs to the **parasympathetic nervous system**, the body's resting nerve system. In well-trained **endurance athletes** the resting pulse is often lower than in untrained people, sometimes under 60 beats per minute.

A permanently slow heartbeat below 60 beats per minute is called **bradycardia**. Brady comes from Greek and means slow. In athletes this can be quite normal. A resting pulse of over 100 beats per minute is called **tachycardia**, from Greek tachy for fast. With fever or exertion a fast pulse is normal, but not at rest.

If the natural timekeeper no longer works properly, a **pacemaker** can help. This is a small device that is placed under the skin. It is connected to the heart by a fine lead. It gives off **electrical impulses** when the heart beats too slowly. Many people live quite normally with one.

gewusst: Over a long life, a heart beats more than two billion times.
If the sinus node fails, the AV node can take over the rhythm, but more slowly.

teile.einleitung: An **eye test** measures how sharply someone sees. This is how you notice whether glasses are needed. There are eye tests for children, adults and, for example, before driving.
wichtigste: An eye test checks how well you see.
How sharply someone sees is called visual acuity.
On the eye chart, the characters get smaller and smaller.
Each eye is checked separately.
With Landolt rings you say where the ring is open.
In Switzerland you need an eye test for the learner driver’s permit.

abschnitte.text: In many eye tests you read characters on an **eye chart** on the wall. The characters get **smaller and smaller** from line to line. The smaller the characters someone can still make out, the better they see. In this way **visual acuity** is measured. It says how finely someone can tell things apart from a certain distance.

In the eye test you usually cover one eye. This way you can test **each eye separately**. Often one eye sees better than the other. You hardly notice this in everyday life, because the better eye makes up for a lot. Only in the test does the difference show.

Instead of letters, **Landolt rings** are often used. Each ring has a small gap. You say whether it is at the top, bottom, left or right. Small children who cannot read yet name **pictures** or show with their hand the direction of characters. This way their eyes too can already be tested well.

abschnitte.titel: Eye test for the driving licence
abschnitte.text: Anyone in Switzerland who wants to learn to drive a car must first take an **eye test**. Only then do you get the **learner driver’s permit**. In road traffic, good sight is especially important. You have to recognise signs, traffic lights and other road users in time. Anyone who needs glasses must wear them when driving.

A simple eye test is done by **opticians**, for example in a glasses shop. For exact examinations and in diseases you go to the **eye doctor**. At school or at the paediatrician, sight is also sometimes checked. Children often do not notice themselves that they see poorly. That is why such tests are especially important.

gewusst: The Landolt rings are named after the Swiss eye doctor Edmund Landolt.
An eye test does not measure only sharpness: there are also tests for colour vision and spatial vision.

teile.einleitung: Trypsin is an enzyme that breaks down proteins from food in the small intestine. It is made in the pancreas, but first in a harmless precursor form. Only in the gut is it switched on.
wichtigste: Trypsin is a digestive enzyme for proteins.
The pancreas makes it as the precursor trypsinogen.
In the duodenum, enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen.
Trypsin cuts protein chains after lysine and arginine.
It belongs to the serine proteases.
It works best at about pH 8.

abschnitte.text: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical processes in the body. Trypsin is a **protease**, that is an enzyme that cuts other proteins into smaller pieces. Proteins consist of long chains of **amino acids**. Trypsin prefers to cut these chains after the amino acids **lysine** and **arginine**. Because it cuts so precisely, it is also happily used in the laboratory.

The **pancreas** does not make trypsin in finished form, but as an inactive precursor, **trypsinogen**. Active trypsin would otherwise attack the tissue of the pancreas itself. For safety there is also an inhibitor there, the **pancreatic trypsin inhibitor SPINK1**. It binds small amounts of trypsin that become active too early. Changes in its gene raise the risk of chronic inflammation of the pancreas.

In the **duodenum**, the enzyme **enteropeptidase**, also called enterokinase, sits in the lining. It cuts a short piece off trypsinogen, and active trypsin is formed. This then activates further precursors, for example **chymotrypsinogen** and procarboxypeptidases. This makes an **activation cascade**: one enzyme switches on many others.

Trypsin belongs to the **serine proteases**. In the active centre, that is the place where it works, sit three amino acids: **serine, histidine and aspartate**. They are called the **catalytic triad**. Aspartate aligns the histidine, the histidine activates the serine, and the serine attacks the bond between two amino acids. Trypsin works best in the slightly basic environment of the small intestine at about **pH 8**.

gewusst: The name trypsin goes back to the German researcher Wilhelm Kühne, who in the 19th century also coined the word “enzyme”.
In laboratories, trypsin is used to detach cells from the bottom of culture dishes so that they can be grown on.

teile.einleitung: Sugary drinks are drinks with a lot of added sugar, for example cola, lemonade or iced tea. They taste good, but often contain more sugar than you might think.
wichtigste: Half a litre of cola contains more than 10 sugar cubes.
Lemonade, cola and iced tea are sugary drinks.
Too much sugar can cause tooth decay.
Water and unsweetened tea are good ways to quench your thirst.
Squash should be diluted strongly with water.
Energy drinks are not suitable for children.

abschnitte.text: Half a litre of ordinary **cola** contains over 50 grams of sugar. That is more than **10 sugar cubes**. **Lemonade** and **iced tea** also contain a lot of added sugar. Because you cannot see the sugar in a drink, it is easy to drink a great deal of it. The fizzy bubbles in many sugary drinks come from **carbon dioxide**.
