wichtigste: Secretin is considered the first hormone to be discovered.
William Bayliss and Ernest Starling identified it in 1902.
It is produced by the S cells of the duodenum.
Acidic food pulp in the duodenum triggers its release.
Secretin stimulates the pancreas to release fluid rich in bicarbonate.
It is made up of 27 amino acids and works via cAMP.

abschnitte.text: In 1902 the British researchers **William Bayliss** and **Ernest Starling** made an important discovery. They showed that a substance from the intestine stimulates the pancreas via the **blood**. Until then, people thought such signals only travelled along nerves. They called the substance **secretin**. It is considered the very first hormone ever discovered.

Secretin is produced by the **S cells** in the lining of the **duodenum**. The duodenum is the first section of the small intestine. When acidic food pulp from the stomach reaches the duodenum, the **pH value** there falls. If it drops below about 4.5, the S cells release secretin into the blood. In this way the intestine reacts directly to stomach acid.

Secretin acts on the **pancreas**. It stimulates the cells of its ducts to release a fluid containing a lot of **bicarbonate**. Bicarbonate is a base and neutralises stomach acid in the intestine. At the same time secretin **inhibits** the release of gastrin and the production of acid in the stomach. This way not too much acid reaches the intestine, and the digestive enzymes can work well.

Secretin is a short **peptide hormone** made of **27 amino acids**. For comparison: insulin consists of 51 amino acids. Secretin is closely related to **glucagon**. The hormones VIP and GIP also belong to the same family. Gastrin and cholecystokinin, on the other hand, form a different family.

The **secretin receptor** sits on the surface of the target cells. It is linked to a **G protein**, which activates adenylate cyclase. As a result, the level of the second messenger **cAMP** rises inside the cell. Among other things, cAMP opens chloride channels. This starts the release of the fluid rich in bicarbonate.

gewusst: The word “hormone” was only coined after secretin was discovered, to name such messenger substances in the blood.
Secretin was therefore the beginning of a completely new field of research, the study of hormones.

teile.einleitung: A **sun hat** protects the head, face and neck from the sun. It helps against sunburn and against overheating. It is particularly important for small children on sunny days.
wichtigste: A sun hat with a wide brim protects the head, face and neck.
The edge of a hat is called the brim.
Light-coloured hats get less hot in the sun.
Protection is most important at midday.
A chin strap holds the hat in place in the wind.
A cap with neck protection has a piece of fabric at the back.

abschnitte.text: The edge that sticks out from a hat is called the **brim**. The wider the brim, the more **shade** it gives. A wide brim protects the **face, ears and neck**. The hat itself covers the head. The brim also keeps light from above away from the eyes, so you are less **dazzled**.

The colour of a hat matters. **Light colours**, for example white, reflect a lot of sunlight. That is why they get less hot in the sun. **Dark colours** absorb the light and warm up a lot. On hot days a light-coloured hat is therefore more comfortable.

A **straw hat** is made of dried, woven stalks. It is light and lets air through, so the head does not sweat. There are also fabric hats that can be washed. A **cap with neck protection** has a piece of fabric hanging down at the back. It protects the neck from sunburn.

Small children should always wear a **head covering** in the sun. Their scalp is often not well covered by hair, and their skin is particularly sensitive. A hat protects against **sunburn** and **overheating**. Many children's sun hats have a **chin strap**. It holds the hat in place even in the wind or while playing.

At **midday** the sun is highest in the sky and shines most strongly. That is when the head needs the most protection. It is best to look for **shade** at this time too. Sun cream and sunglasses help as well. And drinking enough is also important on hot days.

gewusst: In great heat an unprotected head can get sunstroke, and a hat helps to prevent this.
The Panama hat, made of fine plant straw, originally comes from Ecuador, not from Panama.

teile.einleitung: UV filters are the active ingredients in sun creams that protect the skin from ultraviolet radiation. There are mineral and organic filters, and they work in different ways. The sun protection factor shows how strongly a cream protects.
wichtigste: Mineral filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide scatter, reflect and absorb UV.
Organic filters absorb UV and give off the energy as heat.
The sun protection factor compares the sunburn threshold with and without protection.
SPF 30 holds back about 97 per cent of UV-B radiation.
In the laboratory 2 milligrams per square centimetre are applied.
Reapplying keeps up the protection but does not extend it.

abschnitte.text: **Mineral filters** are fine particles, above all **zinc oxide** and **titanium dioxide**. They throw UV radiation back, scatter it and partly absorb it. They are considered well tolerated, but can leave a **white film**. Large particles also scatter visible light. That is why titanium dioxide is often used as **nanoparticles**. Very small particles are almost transparent but still filter UV.

**Organic filters** are molecules that absorb UV photons, that is, take them in. In doing so they enter an **excited state**, a state with more energy. When they fall back, they give off the energy mainly as **heat**. This way the radiation does not reach the skin cells. Good sun creams combine several filters so that they protect against UV-B and UV-A.

The **sun protection factor**, SPF for short, compares the amount of UV that causes slight redness with sun protection to the amount without protection. SPF 20 means that about twenty times more radiation is needed. With **SPF 30** roughly one thirtieth reaches the skin, so about **97 per cent** is intercepted. It is measured with **2 milligrams per square centimetre**. In everyday life most people use much less, and the protection falls.

**Reapplying** replaces cream that has been rubbed or washed off. It does not, however, extend the total protection time. That comes from the skin's own **natural protection time** and the SPF. In the EU **“50+”** is the highest value allowed. Higher numbers would suggest extra performance that hardly exists.

Some organic filters are suspected of harming **corals**. The US state of **Hawaii** therefore decided in 2018, as the first, to ban the sale of sun protection products with **oxybenzone** and **octinoxate**. It came into force in 2021. Whatever the case, clothes, a hat and shade protect reliably and do not end up in the water.

gewusst: An SPF 50 sun protection holds back only a little more UV-B than an SPF 30, namely about 98 instead of 97 per cent.
For the whole body of an adult you need about as much sun cream as fits into a small shot glass.

teile.einleitung: Psoriasis is a skin disease in which reddened, scaly patches appear. It is not contagious and can be treated well today, but usually not cured completely.
wichtigste: The technical term for the disease is psoriasis.
Psoriasis is not contagious.
The immune system wrongly triggers an inflammation in the skin.
The epidermis renews itself far too fast.
Typical are reddened patches with silvery-white scales on the elbows, knees and scalp.
Fingernails and joints can also be affected.
One treatment is UV light therapy.

abschnitte.titel: The immune system makes a mistake
abschnitte.text: The **immune system** normally protects the body from disease-causing agents. In **psoriasis**, though, it wrongly triggers an **inflammation** in the skin. So it is not an infection, and you **cannot catch it** from others. Often psoriasis runs in families. Stress, infections or certain medicines can trigger a new flare-up.

The top layer of skin is called the **epidermis**. It renews itself constantly: new cells grow up from below, old cells fall off at the top as fine flakes. Normally this takes about four weeks. In psoriasis it goes **much too fast**, often in a few days. The cells pile up and form thick, **silvery-white scales** on reddened skin.

Especially often affected are the **elbows**, the **knees** and the **scalp**. The patches have sharp edges and can itch. The **fingernails** often change too: they get small **pits** that look like pinpricks. In some people, **joints** also become inflamed, ache and swell. This is then called psoriatic arthritis.

Psoriasis usually cannot be cured completely, but it can be treated well. Ointments and creams loosen the scales and calm the inflammation. In **UV light therapy**, the skin is irradiated in a targeted way with ultraviolet light. For severe forms there are medicines that slow down the immune system. A skin specialist works with those affected to find the right treatment.

gewusst: Many people with psoriasis notice that their skin gets better in summer with more sun.
The word psoriasis comes from Greek and has to do with itching.

teile.einleitung: Systole is the phase of the heartbeat in which the ventricles contract and pump blood into the body. It is followed by diastole, in which the heart relaxes and fills up again.
wichtigste: Systole means contraction in Greek.
In systole the ventricles pump blood into the large arteries.
It begins with the tensing phase, followed by the ejection phase.
During ejection the aortic and pulmonary valves are open.
At the start of systole you hear the first heart sound.
In systole the pressure in the aorta is at its highest.

abschnitte.text: The word **systole** comes from Greek and means **contraction**. That is exactly what the heart muscle does in this phase. The muscle of the **ventricles** contracts and presses the blood into the large arteries: the left ventricle into the **aorta**, the right into the pulmonary artery. This is followed by **diastole**, in which the muscle relaxes and the ventricles fill up again.

Heart valves work like valves in a pipe and make sure that blood flows in one direction only. During ejection the **semilunar valves** at the exits of the ventricles open, that is the **aortic and pulmonary valves**. The **atrioventricular valves** to the atria are closed so that no blood flows back.

At the start the ventricle muscle tenses, but all the valves are briefly closed. In this **tensing phase** no blood flows out yet, only the pressure rises. As soon as the pressure in the ventricle is higher than in the artery, the valve opens. Now the **ejection phase** begins, and the blood streams out.

At the start of systole the atrioventricular valves close and the heart muscle tenses. This produces the **first heart sound**, which you hear with a stethoscope. When the left ventricle ejects blood, the pressure in the aorta rises to its peak. This **systolic blood pressure** is the first, higher number when blood pressure is measured. An **extrasystole** is an additional, premature heartbeat. Occasional extrasystoles are common and usually harmless.

gewusst: With a blood pressure of 120 over 80, 120 is the systolic value.
The second heart sound is produced when the semilunar valves close at the end of systole.

teile.einleitung: Supercompensation is a model from training science. It explains why training makes us stronger: after exertion the body does not just recover, but builds its performance up a little above the earlier level.
wichtigste: After recovery, performance rises briefly above the starting level.
The phases are exertion, fatigue, recovery and supercompensation.
If the next stimulus comes too late, the gain is lost again.
If it always comes too early, performance gradually falls.
Only stimuli above the threshold trigger an adaptation.
The model is greatly simplified.

abschnitte.text: First comes the **exertion**, for example a run or strength training. During it, performance falls and you are **tired**. During **recovery** the body rebuilds its reserves. After that, performance rises above the starting level for a short time. This raised level is called **supercompensation**. In this way the body prepares itself for the next exertion.

Supercompensation lasts only a limited time. If the next training stimulus comes **far too late**, performance falls back to the starting level. If, on the other hand, the body is put under strain again and again **before** it has recovered, the fatigue adds up. Performance then decreases instead of increasing. That is why **breaks** are just as important as the training itself.

According to the **stimulus threshold rule**, stimuli that are too weak, below the threshold, bring about no adaptation. Stimuli that are too strong can do harm. Only sufficiently strong stimuli **above the threshold** lead to a training effect. After an adaptation, the same stimulus is no longer big enough for the body. That is why the principle of **progressive overload** calls for ever new, slightly higher stimuli.

A well-documented example is **muscle glycogen**, an energy store made of sugar in the muscles. After long endurance exercise and a diet rich in carbohydrates, it fills up beyond its earlier level. **Carb-loading** before a marathon makes use of this: in the days before, you eat a lot of carbohydrates such as pasta and train less.

The model shows everything with a single curve. In reality **energy stores**, **muscles**, **tendons** and the **nervous system** recover at different speeds. That is why supercompensation is considered greatly simplified. Even so, it helps to understand the basic idea: training and recovery belong together.

gewusst: You do not get stronger during training, but during the recovery afterwards.
Tendons and ligaments adapt much more slowly than muscles.

teile.einleitung: Sweating is the way our body cools itself in heat and exertion. Not all living things do it the same way: dogs pant, horses sweat heavily. With a few tricks you also get through hot days well.
wichtigste: A dog hardly sweats and cools itself by panting with its mouth open.
Horses sweat heavily when they gallop fast.
Light, airy clothes are pleasant when sweating in summer.
Anyone who stays in the shade sweats less.
On muggy days sweat hardly dries, which is why you feel sticky.
Against sweat smell, many people use a deodorant.

abschnitte.text: If the body gets too warm, it sends **sweat** onto the skin. When the sweat **evaporates**, it takes heat with it and cools the skin. This keeps body temperature about the same. You sweat in heat, in sport, in fever and sometimes also from excitement. Because you lose water in the process, you have to drink enough.

On **muggy days** the air is very damp. Then it can hardly take up any more water. The **sweat hardly dries** and stays on the skin. That is why you feel **sticky** and are hot despite sweating. In dry heat, on the other hand, sweat evaporates quickly, and you often do not notice at all how much you are sweating.

A **dog** hardly sweats, only a little on the paws. It cools itself by **panting with its mouth open**. In the process, moisture evaporates from the tongue and airways. The **horse**, on the other hand, sweats heavily, especially when it **gallops** fast. Often you then see white foam on its coat. Cats groom themselves and spread saliva over their fur, which cools as it dries.

Anyone who **stays in the shade** sweats less. **Light, airy clothes**, for example of cotton or linen, let the skin breathe. At midday, when the sun is strongest, it is better to avoid great exertion. Against **sweat smell**, regular washing helps. Many people also use a **deodorant** under the armpits.

gewusst: A horse can lose many litres of sweat with great exertion.
Pigs hardly sweat and prefer to cool themselves in a mud puddle.

teile.einleitung: Metabolism is the name for all the chemical processes in the body that turn food into energy and building materials. It takes place in every single cell, day and night. Without metabolism we could neither think nor breathe nor grow.
wichtigste: Metabolism covers the building up and breaking down of substances in the body.
In complete cellular respiration, glucose is broken down into carbon dioxide and water.
When oxygen is short, fermentation in the muscle turns pyruvate into lactate.
Humans store glucose as glycogen in the liver and muscles.
The basal metabolic rate is the energy the body needs at complete rest.
The liver turns poisonous ammonia into urea.
Fat provides about 9 kcal per gram, carbohydrates and protein about 4 kcal.

abschnitte.text: **Metabolism**, in German **“Stoffwechsel”**, covers all the chemical reactions in a living thing. In **breaking down**, nutrients are split up to obtain energy. In **building up**, the body's own substances such as muscle protein or fat are made from them. The reactions are controlled by enzymes and hormones such as insulin. Metabolism runs all the time, even during sleep.

In the **mitochondria**, the power stations of the cell, glucose is burnt with oxygen. At the end of this **cellular respiration**, carbon dioxide and water are produced. The energy released is stored in the molecule ATP, which the cell uses like a battery. We breathe out the carbon dioxide. First the glucose is split into pyruvate in the cytoplasm.

During a fast sprint the muscles do not get enough oxygen. Then they turn pyruvate into **lactate** through **lactic acid fermentation**. This way they quickly gain a little energy, but much less than with oxygen. The lactate is later used further, mainly in the liver and the heart. Yeasts carry out a similar fermentation and produce alcohol and carbon dioxide.

The body stores surplus glucose as **glycogen** in the liver and muscles. When the stores are full, extra energy is stored as fat. When protein is broken down, poisonous ammonia is produced. The **liver** turns it into urea, which the kidneys get rid of in the urine. This makes the liver one of the most important centres of metabolism.

The **basal metabolic rate** is the energy the body needs at complete rest for the heartbeat, breathing and body heat. In adults it is roughly 1,300 to 1,800 kilocalories per day. On top of that comes the energy used for movement and work. Fat provides 9 kcal per gram, carbohydrates and protein about 4 kcal each. A snack with 10 g of fat and 20 g of carbohydrates therefore provides about 90 plus 80, that is 170 kcal.

begriffe.erklaerung: The breaking down of glucose with oxygen to obtain energy in the cell.
The storage form of glucose in the liver and muscles.
A substance formed from pyruvate in the muscle when oxygen is short.
The energy the body needs at complete rest.
A unit of measurement for the energy in food.

gewusst: The brain makes up only about two per cent of body weight, but uses around a fifth of the energy at rest.
Relative to their weight, children need more energy than adults, because they are growing.
The name lactate comes from the Latin word lac for milk, because lactic acid was first discovered in sour milk.

teile.einleitung: Trace elements are substances that the body needs only in very small amounts but without which it cannot stay healthy. They include, for example, iron, iodine, zinc, copper, selenium and fluoride. We take them in with our food.
wichtigste: The body needs trace elements only in tiny amounts.
**Iron** is found in the red blood pigment haemoglobin and helps to carry oxygen.
Lack of iron often leads to anaemia and tiredness.
Without enough **iodine** the thyroid gland grows larger and a **goitre** forms.
Switzerland introduced iodised table salt in 1922.
**Fluoride** protects tooth enamel from decay.
**Zinc** helps the immune system, and **selenium** is found especially in Brazil nuts.

abschnitte.text: The body needs many minerals. Some of them, such as calcium, in large amounts. Others only in **traces**, often a few milligrams or even millionths of a gram per day. These are called **trace elements**. Many are part of **enzymes** or hormones that carry out important work in the body. Too little of them makes you ill, but too much can also do harm.

In the red blood pigment **haemoglobin**, an iron atom binds the oxygen. This way the blood can carry oxygen from the lungs to all parts of the body. If iron is lacking, the body makes too little haemoglobin. You become pale, tired and less able to perform, and this is called **anaemia**. **Copper**, the metal used in electric cables, is also a trace element. It is part of important enzymes, for example for making blood. Lead, mercury and cadmium, by contrast, are poisonous heavy metals.

The **thyroid gland** in the neck needs iodine for its hormones. If iodine is lacking, it grows in order to catch more iodine, and a **goitre** forms. The soils in the Alps are rather poor in iodine, which is why many people in Switzerland used to suffer from a lack of iodine. In **1922** Switzerland was one of the first countries to introduce **iodised table salt**. Since then goitre has become much rarer. A good natural source of iodine is **sea fish** and seaweed, because sea water contains iodine.

**Fluoride** hardens tooth enamel and makes it more resistant to acids. That is why it is in many toothpastes, and in Switzerland there is also fluoridated table salt. **Zinc** takes part in many enzymes and supports the immune defence and wound healing. Good sources are oysters, meat, cheese and wholegrain foods. **Selenium** is found in particularly large amounts in **Brazil nuts**. They grow in South America on soils that contain selenium.

gewusst: Just a few Brazil nuts can cover the daily need for selenium.
The whole body of an adult contains only a few grams of iron, about as much as in a small nail.

teile.einleitung: You need a handkerchief to blow your nose, above all when you have a cold. In Switzerland people often call it a “Nastuch”. Used properly, it helps to stop germs from being passed on.
wichtigste: In Switzerland a handkerchief is often called a “Nastuch”.
Disposable tissues are made of soft paper.
You use a paper tissue only once.
You blow one nostril after the other.
After blowing your nose you wash your hands.
Used tissues contain germs.

abschnitte.text: It is best to blow **one nostril after the other**. You hold one nostril closed and blow gently through the other. That way you do not push the mucus into your ears. With a **cold** your nose often runs, and then you need a lot of tissues. Afterwards you **wash your hands**, because germs get onto your fingers when you blow your nose.

**Disposable tissues** are made of soft, absorbent paper. That is why they are also called **paper handkerchiefs**. They are meant for **single use**. For the next time you take a fresh one and throw the old one in the bin. In the past, people mainly used handkerchiefs made of **cloth**, which are washed again and again. In Switzerland a handkerchief is often called a **“Nastuch”**.

There can be **viruses** and **bacteria** in nasal mucus. That is why you do not touch other people's used tissues, otherwise you can catch something. If you do not have a tissue to hand, it is best to sneeze or cough into the **crook of your elbow** instead of into your hand. That way fewer germs end up on door handles or toys.

To have fresh tissues with you when you are out and about, you put a small **pack** in your pocket or school bag. The pack keeps the tissues clean and dry. You can take it anywhere, to school, on trips or to training.

gewusst: A used paper tissue belongs in the rubbish bin, not in the waste paper.
When you sneeze, the air can shoot out of the nose and mouth at great speed.

teile.einleitung: A tattoo is a picture or pattern that is pricked into the skin with ink so that it lasts for good. People have been tattooing themselves for thousands of years. Because the skin is injured in the process, a fresh tattoo needs care.
wichtigste: The ink is pricked into the dermis.
Scavenger cells take up the ink and hold on to it.
Ötzi has more than 60 tattoos.
The word tattoo comes from Polynesia.
Among the Māori, face tattoos have a long tradition.
Tattoos are usually removed with a laser.

abschnitte.text: When tattooing, a fine needle pricks the skin very many times and brings ink in as it does so. The ink has to reach the **dermis**, the layer under the outer skin. If it lay only in the **epidermis**, it would flake off after a few weeks, because this layer constantly renews itself. In the dermis, **scavenger cells**, also called macrophages, take up the particles of ink. Because they cannot break them down, the picture stays visible.

The glacier mummy **Ötzi** from the Ötztal Alps is over 5,000 years old. More than 60 tattoos made of lines and crosses were found on his skin. The word “tattoo” goes back to **“tatau”** from Tahiti in Polynesia. Sailors around **James Cook** brought it to Europe in the 18th century. Among the **Māori** in New Zealand the traditional tattoos are called **Tā moko**. They show a person's origin and standing.

In tattooing the skin is injured thousands of times. A fresh tattoo is therefore a **wound** that first has to heal. Until then you should not go swimming and should not expose the tattoo to the sun. Germs in the water can cause infections, and sunlight can damage the ink. Later on, too, sun cream protects the tattoo from fading.

A **henna tattoo** is a painted design that disappears after a while. Henna only stains the upper layers of the skin and fades after a few weeks. There are warnings about so-called “black henna” with added substances, because it can cause allergies. A real tattoo is today usually removed with a **laser**. The light breaks up the particles of ink, which the body then gradually clears away. This usually takes several sessions.

gewusst: Ötzi's tattoos are often on joints and on the back. Researchers suspect that they may have been used to treat pain.
Removing a tattoo usually takes much longer and costs more than getting it.

teile.einleitung: The skeleton is the sturdy framework of bones that supports, protects and moves the body. An adult human has around 206 bones, from the tiny stirrup in the ear to the long thigh bone. Bones are not dead material but living tissue.
wichtigste: The skeleton supports the body and protects important organs.
The longest human bone is the thigh bone.
The smallest bone is the stirrup in the middle ear.
A human normally has 12 pairs of ribs.
Blood cells are made in the red bone marrow.
The mineral calcium makes bones hard and strong.
Many animals have an internal skeleton, whereas insects have an external skeleton.

abschnitte.text: The skeleton gives the body its shape and holds it upright. It **protects** delicate organs: the skull surrounds the brain, and the ribcage protects the heart and lungs. Together with the muscles it makes every **movement** possible. Calcium is also stored in the bones. And inside many bones our blood is made.

The longest bone is the **thigh bone**, which makes up about a quarter of a person's height. It is also one of the strongest bones and carries the weight of the body. The smallest bone is the **stirrup** in the middle ear, which measures only about three millimetres. The ribcage consists of the spine, the breastbone and 12 pairs of ribs. Each hand alone contains 27 bones.

On the outside bones are hard and solid, and inside many have a sponge-like framework. In between lies the **bone marrow**. In the red bone marrow, billions of new **blood cells** are made every day. In adults it is found mainly in the pelvis, breastbone, ribs and vertebrae. Yellow bone marrow consists mainly of fat.

Bones consist largely of minerals, above all **calcium** and phosphate. They make the bone hard, while protein fibres keep it flexible. Dairy products, green vegetables and nuts provide a lot of calcium. **Vitamin D**, which the skin makes with sunlight, helps the body to absorb the calcium. Exercise and sport make the bones even stronger.

Vertebrates such as fish, birds and mammals have an **internal skeleton** with a backbone. Insects, spiders and crustaceans, on the other hand, wear an **external skeleton** made of a hard shell. To be able to grow, they have to moult. Sharks and rays have a skeleton made of cartilage instead of bone. Like humans, a giraffe has only seven neck vertebrae.

begriffe.erklaerung: Soft tissue inside the bones in which blood cells are made.
A mineral that makes bones and teeth hard.
A framework of bones inside the body, as in humans.
A hard shell on the outside of the body, as in insects.

gewusst: Babies are born with considerably more bones than adults, because some only fuse together later.
Bones are constantly being rebuilt, so the skeleton is renewed again and again over the years.
Relative to its weight, the thigh bone can carry very heavy loads.

teile.einleitung: A sense is the ability of a living thing to perceive stimuli from the environment or from its own body. Traditionally, humans are said to have five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. Only the brain turns the signals from the sense organs into a picture of the world.
wichtigste: A sense is the ability to perceive certain stimuli.
Traditionally, humans are said to have five senses.
Each sense has its own sense organ with specialised sensory cells.
Sensory cells turn stimuli such as light or sound into nerve signals.
Perception only comes about in the brain.
Today further senses are known, such as the sense of balance.
Some animals have senses that humans lack.

abschnitte.text: A sense allows us to take in information from our surroundings. This needs a **stimulus**, for example light, sound, a smell or a touch. Certain **sensory cells** react to exactly this stimulus. They sit in the sense organs such as the eye, ear, nose, tongue and skin. Without senses we would know nothing about the world around us.

More than 2,300 years ago the Greek philosopher **Aristotle** already described five senses. These are sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. This division is still taught in school today. Sight gives us the most information about our surroundings. The sense of smell is closely linked to memories and feelings.

When a stimulus reaches a sensory cell, the cell produces an electrical **nerve signal**. The signal travels along nerves to the **brain**. There it is processed, compared with memories and interpreted. Only then do we recognise, for example, a face or a song. That is why the brain can also be fooled, for example by **optical illusions**.

Science today knows more than five senses. The **sense of balance** in the inner ear tells us whether we are standing upright. The sense of temperature and the sense of pain are often counted as part of touch. With **proprioception** we feel where our arms and legs are at the moment, even with our eyes closed. Depending on how you count, you can arrive at nine or even more senses.

Many animals have senses that far exceed ours. Dogs smell much better than humans, and eagles see very sharply over great distances. Bats find their way with **ultrasound** and hear the echo of their calls. Migratory birds can sense the Earth's **magnetic field**. Sharks even detect weak electric fields given off by their prey.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something from the environment that a sense organ can perceive, such as light or sound.
A part of the body with which we perceive something, for example the eye or ear.
A special cell that turns a stimulus into a nerve signal.
The recognising and interpreting of sense impressions in the brain.

gewusst: A large part of our cerebral cortex is busy processing visual stimuli.
Much of what we experience as the taste of food actually comes from the nose.
People without sight often learn to perceive particularly finely with touch and hearing.

teile.einleitung: A syncope is a brief faint. You lose consciousness for a few seconds because the brain briefly gets too little blood, and you usually recover quickly afterwards.
wichtigste: Syncope is the technical term for a brief faint.
The cause is a short reduction of blood flow to the brain.
A faint usually lasts only seconds to a few minutes.
Standing for a long time in great heat can bring on a faint.
Your vision going black is a typical warning sign.
You lay the person flat and raise their legs.

abschnitte.text: In a **syncope**, the brain briefly gets too little blood. As a result it lacks oxygen, and you lose consciousness for a moment. The term comes from Greek. Typically you come round again by yourself after seconds or a few minutes. If the unconsciousness lasts longer, medical help is needed.

A faint happens especially easily when **standing for a long time in great heat**. The blood vessels widen, and blood collects in the legs. Some people faint at the sight of blood or when they are in pain. In this **vasovagal syncope** the nervous system reacts too strongly, and pulse and blood pressure suddenly drop.

Before a faint, **dizziness**, **blackouts of vision**, nausea and sweating often appear. If you notice this, it is best to sit or lie down straight away. That way you can avoid a fall. It also helps to drink enough and to move your leg muscles when standing for a long time.

If someone has fainted briefly and is breathing normally, you lay the person **flat** and **raise their legs**. This lets more blood flow to the heart and the brain, and usually the person comes round quickly. If the person stays unconscious but breathes normally, you put them in the **recovery position**. This keeps the airways clear. Then you call for help, in Switzerland the ambulance service on **144**, and check the breathing.

gewusst: Most faints are harmless, but a first faint should still be checked by a doctor.
If you have to stand for a long time, you can guard against fainting by tensing your leg muscles again and again.

teile.einleitung: Sun cream is a protective product that you put on your skin so that the sun's UV rays do less damage. It protects the skin from sunburn and lowers the risk of skin cancer. How strongly it protects is shown by the sun protection factor on the packaging.
wichtigste: Sun cream protects the skin from sunburn.
It contains UV filters that catch the sun's rays.
The sun protection factor, SPF for short, shows how strongly it protects.
You should apply plenty and reapply regularly.
After swimming you have to apply it again, even with water-resistant cream.
Sun cream is only one part of sun protection, and shade and clothing belong to it too.
A high sun protection factor is recommended for children.

abschnitte.text: Sun cream is a cream, lotion or spray with **UV filters**. These substances catch a large part of the UV radiation before it can damage the skin. In this way sun cream protects against sunburn and long-term skin damage. But it does not replace shade. Good sun creams protect against both **UV-B** and **UV-A**.

There are two kinds of filter. **Mineral filters** such as zinc oxide or titanium dioxide act like tiny mirrors and reflect the radiation. **Chemical filters** absorb the radiation and turn it into heat. Many products combine both kinds. For the cream to work, it has to form an even layer on the skin.

The **sun protection factor** says how much longer you could stay in the sun with cream than without it. An SPF of 30 keeps out about 97 per cent of UV-B radiation, an SPF of 50 about 98 per cent. But these values only apply if you use enough cream. For an adult that is about three tablespoons for the whole body. For children and in the mountains SPF 30 or 50 is recommended.

It is best to put on cream before going outside. Ears, nose, the back of the neck and feet are often forgotten. After swimming, sweating or drying yourself with a towel you have to **reapply**. Even a **water-resistant** cream loses part of its effect in water. Reapplying does not make the protection last longer, it only keeps it up.

The first sun protection products came on the market as early as the 1930s and 1940s. A well-known figure is the Austrian chemist **Franz Greiter**, who developed a sun cream after getting sunburnt on Piz Buin. Piz Buin lies in the Silvretta range on the border between the Grisons and Austria, and the Piz Buin brand came out in 1946. Greiter later also made the **sun protection factor** widely known. Today we know that some filter substances can harm coral reefs, which is why Hawaii, for example, has banned certain substances.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance in sun cream that catches UV rays.
A number that shows how well a sun cream protects against sunburn.
A cream that keeps part of its protection even after a short swim.
A white mineral that reflects the sun's rays.

gewusst: Most people apply much less sun cream than needed and so get only part of the protection stated.
A well-known sun cream is named after a mountain on the border between the Grisons and Austria.
Sun cream can go out of date, which is why the packaging says how long it keeps after opening.

teile.einleitung: The ankle joint connects the lower leg with the foot. It is also simply called the ankle. We need it with every step, when running, jumping and balancing.
wichtigste: The ankle joint lies between the lower leg and the foot.
The two knobs on the left and right are called the **inner ankle bone** and the **outer ankle bone**.
The **talus** sits between the two ankle bones.
When you twist your ankle, it is usually the **outer ligaments** that are injured.
The **Achilles tendon** runs at the back over the joint to the heel.
Balancing on one leg strengthens the ankles.
High walking boots give the joint support when hiking in the mountains.

abschnitte.text: In the ankle joint three bones meet: the **shinbone**, the **fibula** and the **talus**. The lower ends of the shinbone and the fibula form the two **ankle knobs**. On the inside is the inner ankle bone, on the outside the outer ankle bone. Between them the talus sits as if held in a clamp. The whole weight of the body passes through these bones into the foot. A distinction is made between an **upper** and a **lower ankle joint**.

The upper ankle joint raises and lowers the foot. When you stand on **tiptoe**, it stretches the foot downwards. The joint makes this movement together with the **calf muscles**. The strength of the calf is passed to the heel bone through the **Achilles tendon**. It is the strongest tendon in the body. The lower ankle joint lets the foot tilt inwards and outwards, for example on uneven ground.

Strong **ligaments** hold the joint together. Usually the foot turns over inwards, so that the outer side is overstretched. That is why the **outer ligaments** are most often injured when you twist your ankle. They can be overstretched or tear. The joint swells up and hurts. Cooling, raising the foot and rest help. If the pain is severe, you have the foot examined by a doctor.

When **balancing** on one leg, many small muscles around the ankle work. This makes it more stable, and you do not twist it so easily. You can stand on one leg while brushing your teeth, for example. When **hiking in the mountains** on stony paths, high walking boots protect you. They reach above the ankle and give the joint support.

gewusst: When running and jumping, the ankle joint has to withstand many times the body's weight.
Not a single muscle is attached directly to the talus.

teile.einleitung: Stress is the body's reaction to strain and danger. In the short term it makes us more capable, but it can do harm if it lasts a very long time.
wichtigste: In danger the body prepares for fight or flight.
Pulse, breathing and muscle tension all rise.
The sympathetic nervous system gets the body ready to perform.
Cortisol is an important stress hormone when stress lasts longer.
Positive stress is called eustress, and stress that weighs you down is called distress.
Hans Selye made the term stress well known in medicine.
Exercise, sleep and breaks help against stress.

abschnitte.text: Even our ancestors had to react at lightning speed in danger. That is why there is the ancient **fight-or-flight response**. The pulse gets faster, you breathe more quickly and the muscles tense up. The brain is wide awake. This gives the body a lot of strength in a short time. Today it is more likely to be exams, arguments or time pressure that trigger this reaction.

During stress the **sympathetic nervous system** becomes active, part of the autonomic nervous system. It acts like an accelerator. The **parasympathetic nervous system** then brings back calm and recovery. In addition, the adrenal glands release hormones. Adrenaline acts immediately, while **cortisol** from the adrenal cortex provides energy when stress lasts longer.

Not all stress is bad. We experience **eustress** as stimulating, for example before a competition or a performance. **Distress**, on the other hand, weighs us down and makes us restless. The **Yerkes-Dodson law** of 1908 describes how a medium level of tension often leads to the best performance. Too little and too much tension make performance worse.

From the 1930s the doctor **Hans Selye** studied how the body reacts to strain. He took over the English word stress, which originally came from engineering and means pressure or tension. In this way he shaped today's idea of stress in medicine.

If stress lasts a long time, the stress hormones stay high. This can weaken the **immune system**, and you get ill more easily. Sleep problems and headaches can also develop. Regular **exercise** breaks down stress hormones and lifts your mood. Enough sleep, breaks and talking with friends or family also help.

gewusst: The word stress originally comes from materials science, where it described the strain on a material.
Even a short walk can help to reduce tension.

teile.einleitung: We dream every night, even if we often no longer remember it in the morning. Dreams are pictures, stories and feelings that our brain creates during sleep. Some are funny, some strange and some frightening.
wichtigste: All people dream every night.
Most dreams are forgotten a few minutes after waking up.
A dream that frightens you is called a nightmare.
In a lucid dream you realise that you are dreaming.
In daydreaming the thoughts wander although you are awake.
Dogs also have a dreaming phase in their sleep.

abschnitte.text: Sleep consists of several phases. We dream most vividly in **REM sleep**. REM stands for “rapid eye movement”, because the eyes move back and forth under the eyelids. This phase occurs several times in a night. **All people** dream, even those who think they never dream.

Most dreams are forgotten after **a few minutes**. You remember best if you wake up straight out of a dream. If you want to keep your dreams, put a notebook next to the bed and **write them down straight away**. Such a notebook is called a dream diary.

A **nightmare** is an unpleasant dream from which you often wake up frightened. Then it helps to switch on a light for a moment and to tell yourself that it was only a dream. In a **lucid dream**, by contrast, you know that you are dreaming. Some people can then even steer their dream. In **daydreaming** you are awake, and your thoughts still wander to imagined things.

Many animals also have a dreaming phase. In a **dog** you can see this clearly: in sleep its paws sometimes twitch, or it barks softly. What animals dream, however, nobody knows exactly, because they cannot tell us.

People have always asked themselves what dreams mean. The **dreamcatcher** comes from the indigenous peoples of **North America**. According to their belief, it is meant to keep bad dreams away. Around 1900 the doctor **Sigmund Freud** wrote a famous book about the interpretation of dreams. Today scientists research dreams in **sleep laboratories**.

gewusst: In REM sleep most muscles are as if paralysed. This is why we do not act out our dreams with our bodies.
Noises from the surroundings, such as an alarm clock, can be built into a dream.

teile.einleitung: The eye supplies only signals, the pictures arise in the brain. Responsible for this is the **visual cortex** at the back of the head. It processes the signals from the eyes into what we consciously see.
wichtigste: The visual cortex lies in the occipital lobe of the cerebrum.
It processes the signals from the eyes into pictures.
The primary visual cortex is called V1 in technical language.
The signals are switched over in the thalamus beforehand.
The right visual cortex processes the left visual field.
If both visual cortices are damaged, you can be blind despite healthy eyes.

abschnitte.text: The eye turns light into electrical signals. Only the **visual cortex** makes pictures from them that we perceive consciously. It lies in the **occipital lobe**, that is, in the rear part of the cerebrum. The first station is called the **primary visual cortex**, or **V1** for short. V stands for visual, that is, concerning sight. Similarly, the auditory cortex is called A1 and the cortex for movement M1.

The signals run from the eye on via the optic nerve and the optic chiasm. In the **thalamus**, a relay station in the diencephalon, they are switched over in the lateral geniculate nucleus. After that they travel as the **optic radiation** to the visual cortex. Because the visual pathway partly crosses, everything from the **left visual field** ends up in the right visual cortex. The right visual field is processed on the left.

The lens in the eye produces an **upside-down picture** on the retina. Even so, we see the world upright. Our visual system has learned to interpret the picture correctly. We do not notice the **blind spot** either. The brain fills the gap with the surroundings and with the pictures from the other eye.

The researchers **David Hubel** and **Torsten Wiesel** studied how nerve cells of the visual cortex work. They found out that many cells respond to particular shapes, for example to **edges** and **lines** in a particular direction. From many such simple building blocks, the brain puts together whole pictures. For this research they received the Nobel Prize in 1981.

If both visual cortices are damaged, for example by a stroke, a person can become **blind** although their eyes are healthy. This is called **cortical blindness**. The signals do arrive, but can no longer be processed into pictures. If only one side is affected, usually one half of the visual field is lost. This shows how important the brain is for seeing.

gewusst: A large part of the cerebral cortex is wholly or partly occupied with seeing.
Besides V1 there are other visual areas that process, for example, colours or movements in particular.

teile.einleitung: The autonomic nervous system controls all body functions that run automatically, without our thinking about them. It regulates heartbeat, breathing, digestion and sweating. Its two most important parts, the sympathetic and the parasympathetic nervous system, work like an accelerator and a brake.
wichtigste: The autonomic nervous system works largely independently of our will.
It is also called the vegetative nervous system.
The sympathetic nervous system activates the body, the parasympathetic relaxes it.
The sympathetic nervous system prepares us for fight or flight.
The parasympathetic nervous system provides rest, recovery and digestion.
A third part controls the gut directly.
Stress and relaxation affect the whole body through this nervous system.

abschnitte.text: Our nervous system has two large areas. With the **somatic nervous system** we consciously control our skeletal muscles, for example when running. The **autonomic nervous system**, by contrast, looks after everything that happens by itself. It regulates heartbeat, blood pressure, breathing, digestion, body temperature and much more. Important control centres lie in the brain stem and in the hypothalamus.

The **sympathetic nervous system** is the body's accelerator. It becomes active with excitement, fear or effort. Then the heart beats faster, the airways widen and the pupils become larger. Digestion is slowed, because the energy is needed for the muscles. Experts call this the **fight-or-flight reaction**.

The **parasympathetic nervous system** is the brake and provides rest and recovery. It slows the heartbeat and stimulates digestion. The most important nerve of this system is the **vagus nerve**, which runs from the brain stem to the abdomen. After a large meal the parasympathetic nervous system is especially active. That is why we often feel tired and full then.

The sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems are **opposites** and act in opposite ways on many organs. Normally both are active at the same time, only sometimes one dominates and sometimes the other. This is how the body constantly adapts to the situation. In addition there is the **enteric nervous system** in the gut wall, which is sometimes called the belly brain. It controls the movements of the gut largely independently.

Before an exam your heart pounds and your hands get damp, that is the sympathetic nervous system. Blushing or a queasy feeling in your stomach is also linked to the autonomic nervous system. When you breathe deeply and slowly, you can stimulate the parasympathetic nervous system and calm down. Constant stress can disturb the balance and lead to headaches or sleep problems. Exercise, enough sleep and breaks help you to get back into **balance**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of the autonomic nervous system that activates the body.
The part of the autonomic nervous system that provides rest and recovery.
The most important nerve of the parasympathetic system, which supplies many organs.
Independent, without conscious control.

gewusst: In the gut there are many millions of nerve cells, about as many as in the spinal cord.
The word vegetative comes from the Latin vegetare, which means to enliven.
Goosebumps from fear or from hearing beautiful music are set off by the sympathetic nervous system.

teile.einleitung: Suva is the largest accident insurer in Switzerland. It mainly insures employees in industry, trades and construction against accidents and occupational diseases, and works hard to prevent accidents.
wichtigste: Suva stands for Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund.
Its head office is in Lucerne.
It covers accidents at work, accidents outside work and occupational diseases.
From 8 hours a week, leisure accidents are insured too.
The daily allowance is 80 per cent of the insured earnings.
Suva returns surpluses through lower premiums.
Prevention, insurance and rehabilitation are its three pillars.

abschnitte.text: **Suva**, the **Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund**, has its head office in **Lucerne** and agencies all over Switzerland. It is an independent organisation under public law and **not profit-oriented**. It returns surpluses to the insured people as lower premiums. Those insured are mainly employees in industry, trades and construction.

The compulsory accident insurance under the **Accident Insurance Act** (UVG) covers accidents at work, accidents in leisure time and **occupational diseases**. Ordinary illnesses are covered by health insurance. Anyone who works **at least eight hours a week** for the same employer is also insured for leisure accidents. Below that, only accidents at work are covered.

The accident insurance pays the treatment costs. If someone cannot work, there is a **daily allowance**. In the case of full incapacity for work it is **80 per cent** of the insured earnings and is paid out after a short waiting period. Suva runs two **rehabilitation clinics**: in **Bellikon** in the canton of Aargau and in **Sion** in the Valais. There people who have had accidents learn to return to everyday life and work.

Besides insurance, Suva takes care of **prevention**. It advises companies, checks workplace safety in many industries and runs campaigns, including on leisure accidents in sport. Prevention, insurance and rehabilitation are its three pillars.

The highest governing body is the **Suva Council** with 40 seats. 16 belong to employers' organisations, 16 to employees' organisations and 8 to the federal government. The members are elected by the **Federal Council** for four years. In this way employers, employees and the federal government decide on Suva together.

gewusst: At Suva, employers and employees sit at the same table with equal strength.
Apprentices are also insured against accidents through their company from their very first day of work.

teile.einleitung: **Heartburn** is a burning feeling behind the breastbone. It happens when stomach acid flows back into the oesophagus. Almost everyone has it now and then, and it is usually harmless.
wichtigste: In heartburn, stomach acid flows back into the oesophagus.
It is typically felt behind the breastbone.
Normally a ring muscle prevents the backflow.
Large, fatty meals and lying down after eating encourage heartburn.
Antacids neutralise stomach acid.
In medicine the backflow is called reflux.

abschnitte.text: In the stomach, food is mixed with strong **stomach acid**. The stomach lining is protected against this acid. The lining of the **oesophagus** is not. If acidic stomach contents get back into the oesophagus, it burns. In medicine this backflow is called **reflux**, from the Latin word for flowing back.

Heartburn is typically felt **behind the breastbone**. That is where the oesophagus runs. Sometimes the burning rises up into the **throat**. Often there is also a sour taste in the mouth. If reflux happens often and causes problems, it is called **reflux disease**.

Where the oesophagus joins the stomach there is a ring of muscle. This is the **lower oesophageal sphincter**. It opens when we swallow and closes again afterwards. In this way it stops stomach contents from flowing back. If it does not close properly, acid can rise up.

**Very fatty food** stays in the stomach for a long time and can loosen the ring muscle. Spicy food, coffee and chocolate can also cause problems. **Large meals** increase the pressure in the stomach. Anyone who **lies down** straight afterwards makes it easier for the acid to travel upwards. Smaller portions and some time before going to bed are better.

Against heartburn at night it helps to **raise the upper body in bed**. Then the acid has to rise against **gravity**, which it manages much less well. **Acid-binding medicines**, known as **antacids**, contain alkaline substances. They neutralise part of the stomach acid. If heartburn happens very often, you should get medical advice.

gewusst: The “Sod” in the German word for heartburn, “Sodbrennen”, is an old word meaning something like “welling up” or “boiling”.
Stomach acid is so acidic that it kills many bacteria in food.

teile.einleitung: Training makes you strong and gives you stamina, but only with enough recovery. Someone who trains too much over a long time and rests too little can fall into overtraining. Then performance falls instead of rising.
wichtigste: In overtraining syndrome, performance falls persistently.
The cause is too much strain with too little recovery.
Tiredness, poor sleep and irritability are typical.
A resting pulse that stays raised for days can be a warning sign.
The most important measure is to cut training down sharply.
Recovery can take weeks to months.

abschnitte.text: In training the body is challenged. In the **recovery** afterwards, it adapts and becomes more capable. In **overtraining syndrome** this balance is wrong for a longer time. Performance falls despite the training, or precisely because of it. It does not recover even after a few days of rest.

Not every tiredness is overtraining. Sometimes people deliberately train very hard, for example at a training camp. If performance recovers within days to weeks afterwards, it is called **functional overreaching**. After the break you are often even better than before. In true overtraining this is not so.

**Persistent tiredness**, **sleep disturbances**, irritability and a falling desire for sport are typical. Overtrained athletes also often fall ill more often, because their **defences** are weakened. Many measure their **resting pulse** in the morning after waking up. If it is clearly higher than usual for several days, this can point to insufficient recovery. Experts distinguish two forms: the rather restless **sympathetic form** and the rather listless **parasympathetic form** with a low resting pulse.

The most important measure is to **cut training down clearly** and give the body rest. This includes plenty of **sleep**, a balanced diet and less stress. A pronounced overtraining often needs **weeks to months** to heal fully. That is why prevention is so important: a good training plan always contains rest days and lighter weeks.

gewusst: Muscles do not get stronger during training, but in the recovery time afterwards.
Stress at school or at work can also contribute to the body recovering less well from training.

teile.einleitung: The lower jaw is the large bone that shapes the bottom of your face. It is the only bone in the head that can move. Without it we could not chew, bite or speak.
wichtigste: The lower jaw is the only movable bone in the head.
It is the largest and strongest bone in the face.
The lower teeth are set in it.
The jaw joint lies in front of the ear.
Seen from above, the lower jaw looks like a horseshoe.
At the front it forms the chin.

abschnitte.text: The bones of the skull have grown firmly together. Only the **lower jaw**, called the **mandible** in technical language, can move through a joint. It is the **largest and strongest** bone in the face. It has to withstand a lot when biting. When you open your mouth, the lower jaw swings **down**, and the upper jaw stays fixed to the skull.

If you look at the lower jaw from above, it looks like a **horseshoe**. At the front it is curved round, at the back it has two ends that rise upwards. At the front it comes together in the **chin**, which you can easily feel. At the top back it forms the **jaw joint** with the skull. If you put your fingers in front of your ears and open your mouth, you feel it move.

In the lower jaw are set the **lower teeth** with their roots. The upper teeth sit in the upper jaw. Children first have **milk teeth**, and later the permanent teeth grow in. An adult has up to 32 teeth including the wisdom teeth, so up to 16 in the lower jaw. When chewing, the lower jaw moves up and down and a little to the side. This is how the teeth grind up the food.

You need the lower jaw for **chewing** and for **speaking**. Strong **chewing muscles** pull it upwards and press the teeth together. You can feel the largest of them in your cheek when you bite down hard. When you speak, the lower jaw is constantly moving a little, so that the tongue and lips can form the sounds.

gewusst: A chewing muscle, the masseter, is among the strongest muscles of the body in proportion to its size.
In finds of early humans, lower jaws are often well preserved, because they are so strongly built.

teile.einleitung: Forearm crutches, often simply called crutches, help you to walk when a leg is injured. You support yourself with your hands and forearms and put less weight on the injured leg. This lets it heal better.
wichtigste: You often need crutches when a leg is injured.
Usually you use two crutches.
You support yourself on your hands and forearms.
At the bottom, a rubber tip stops them from slipping.
Going up stairs, the healthy leg goes first.
The length can be adjusted.

abschnitte.text: Someone who has broken a leg, sprained a foot or had an operation on the knee often may not put full weight on the leg. With **crutches** the injured leg has to carry less weight. This lets it **heal** better. Usually you walk with **two crutches**, one in each hand. This makes you steadier, and the weight is spread well on both sides.

On a **forearm crutch** you hold a **handle** with your hand, and the forearm rests in a **cuff**. That is where the name comes from. At the bottom the crutch has a **rubber tip**. It grips the ground well and stops the crutch from slipping. If the tip is worn, you should replace it. In wet weather, leaves or snow you have to be especially careful.

Crutches have holes and a button with which you can adjust the **length**. This way they fit tall and short people. When you stand upright and let your arms hang, the handles should be about at the height of the **wrists**. Then the elbow is slightly bent when walking. It is best if a professional in the hospital or in physiotherapy adjusts the crutches.

There is a simple rule for climbing stairs. **Going up**, the **healthy leg** goes first, because it has to lift the body. The crutches and the injured leg follow afterwards. **Going down** it is the other way round: first come the crutches and the injured leg, then the healthy one. If there is a handrail, you hold on to it with one hand.

gewusst: A memory rhyme for the stairs goes: the good goes up, the bad goes down.
Walking with crutches is tiring. Many people afterwards feel muscles in their arms and shoulders that they otherwise hardly use.

teile.einleitung: Sports medicine deals with the health of people who do sport. It helps to prevent and treat injuries and studies how the body reacts to training. The fight against doping is part of it too.
wichtigste: A **resting ECG** can detect heart diseases and rhythm disorders.
**Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** is considered a common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.
In **exercise-induced asthma** the airways narrow because of exertion.
A **stress fracture** results from repeated overloading.
Too much plain water during long runs can cause a dangerous lack of sodium.
Altitude training stimulates the production of red blood cells.
**WADA** publishes the list of banned substances every year, and in Switzerland **Swiss Sport Integrity** carries out checks.

abschnitte.titel: Keeping an eye on the heart
abschnitte.text: In sports medical examinations a **resting ECG** is often done. It records the electrical activity of the heart. This can reveal certain heart diseases that can become dangerous during sport. One of them is **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy**: here the heart muscle is abnormally thickened. It can go unnoticed for a long time and cause dangerous rhythm disorders under strain. It is considered a common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

In **exercise-induced asthma** the bronchial tubes narrow during or after sport, often in cold, dry air. A good warm-up and medicines prescribed by a doctor help. Many endurance athletes train at **altitude** for periods of time. There the oxygen pressure of the air is lower. The body reacts by making more **red blood cells** and can then carry more oxygen. In Switzerland, places in the Alps, for example, are suitable for this.

A **stress fracture**, also called a fatigue fracture, happens without an accident. Many small strains cause fine cracks in the bone, often in runners in the middle of the foot or the shinbone. Enough recovery between training sessions helps to prevent it. With drinking, too, you can overdo it: anyone who drinks far too much plain water during a long run dilutes their blood. At the same time **sodium** is lost in sweat. This **hyponatraemia** can lead to confusion and in extreme cases to danger to life.

**Doping** means using banned substances or methods to improve performance. The **World Anti-Doping Agency**, WADA for short, publishes the list of banned substances that applies worldwide every year. It was founded in 1999. National bodies and sports federations base their checks on it. In Switzerland **Swiss Sport Integrity** is responsible. This independent foundation carries out doping tests and also deals with ethical violations in sport.

gewusst: A heart that does a lot of endurance training for years can become larger. This is then called an athlete's heart.
Doping tests take place not only at competitions but also unannounced during training.

teile.einleitung: The thalamus is an important relay station deep in the brain. Almost all sensory stimuli pass through it before they reach the cerebral cortex. It filters what we become aware of.
wichtigste: The thalamus is the largest part of the diencephalon.
It filters sensory information and passes it on to the cerebral cortex.
It is also called the “gateway to consciousness”.
Only the sense of smell does not mainly run through the thalamus.
The lateral geniculate nucleus passes signals from the retina to the visual cortex.
The Greek “thalamos” means chamber or bedchamber.

abschnitte.text: The **thalamus** is the largest part of the **diencephalon**. It lies deep inside, between the cerebrum and the brainstem. There are two of them, one in each half of the brain. The name comes from the Greek “thalamos”, which meant an inner room or **bedchamber**. This fits its hidden position deep in the brain.

Almost all sensory stimuli pass through the thalamus on their way to the **cerebral cortex**. It is a **relay station** and filters which information is important. That is why it is also called the “gateway to consciousness”. Only the **sense of smell** is an exception. Smell information travels from the olfactory bulb directly to the olfactory cortex, without first being switched over in the thalamus.

The thalamus is made up of many groups of nerve cells, the **nuclei**. Each has its own jobs. The **lateral geniculate nucleus** receives the fibres of the optic nerve. From there the visual pathways run to the **visual cortex** in the occipital lobe. Other nuclei pass on signals from hearing, touch or taste, or help to control movements.

After a **stroke** in the thalamus, **Dejerine-Roussy syndrome** can develop. People with it suffer severe pain on the opposite side of the body. In the very rare **fatal familial insomnia**, misfolded proteins called prions destroy mainly nuclei of the thalamus. In **essential tremor** the hands shake. In this **deep brain stimulation**, an electrode in a nucleus of the thalamus can greatly reduce the shaking.

gewusst: The thalamus is also involved in sleep and helps to block out stimuli while you sleep.
Because almost all sensory pathways run through it, even small damage in the thalamus can disturb feeling or sight.

teile.einleitung: Sunburn is an inflammation of the skin that happens when you stay in the sun unprotected for too long. It is caused by the invisible UV rays in sunlight. The skin turns red, feels hot and hurts, and sometimes blisters even form.
wichtigste: Anyone who stays in the sun too long can get sunburnt.
It is caused by the sun's UV radiation.
The skin turns red, feels hot and hurts a few hours after sunbathing.
Frequent sunburn increases the risk of skin cancer.
Children's skin is particularly sensitive.
In the mountains and near water the UV radiation is stronger.
Shade, clothing, a hat and sun cream protect you.

abschnitte.text: Sunburn is an **inflammation** of the skin caused by too much sunlight. Experts also call it dermatitis solaris. The first signs usually only appear a few hours after sunbathing. The redness is strongest after about a day. After a few days the burnt skin peels off.

Sunlight contains invisible **UV radiation**. The UV-B rays in particular penetrate the upper layer of the skin and damage the genetic material of the cells there. The body reacts with an inflammation, the blood vessels widen and the skin turns red. As protection the skin makes the brown pigment **melanin**, and we get a tan. But this tan protects only a little.

Every sunburn leaves damage in the skin cells, even when the redness disappears again. Sunburn in childhood above all increases the risk of **skin cancer**. Switzerland is one of the countries with a particularly large number of cases of black skin cancer, called **melanoma**. Too much sun also makes the skin age faster. Severe sunburn can also cause fever and nausea.

The sun is strongest in summer between 11 am and 3 pm. UV radiation increases with every metre of altitude, which is why it is much stronger on the Jungfraujoch than on Lake Zurich. Snow, water and sand reflect the light and increase the effect. You can get sunburnt on cloudy days too. The **UV index** in the weather forecast shows how strong the radiation is.

The best protection is **shade**, especially around midday. A hat, a T-shirt and sunglasses give extra protection. You put sun cream with a high sun protection factor on uncovered skin. If you do get sunburnt, cool compresses, drinking plenty and gels with **aloe vera** help. With blisters or fever you should go to a doctor.

begriffe.erklaerung: An invisible part of sunlight that can damage the skin.
A brown pigment that the skin makes as protection against the sun.
A number that shows how strong the sun's radiation is on a given day.
A dangerous form of skin cancer, also called black skin cancer.

gewusst: Animals with pale skin, such as pigs, can also get sunburnt.
You can also get sunburnt in winter when skiing, because the snow reflects the radiation.
Hardly any UV-B radiation gets through an ordinary window pane, so you rarely get sunburnt behind glass.

teile.einleitung: Ultraviolet radiation, UV radiation for short, is a part of sunlight that we cannot see. It helps the body to make vitamin D. Too much of it, however, harms the skin and eyes.
wichtigste: UV radiation is invisible to our eyes.
Most UV radiation comes from the sun.
Too much UV radiation leads to sunburn.
Part of the radiation also comes through clouds.
In the mountains the UV radiation is stronger.
The ozone layer holds back a lot of UV radiation.

abschnitte.text: Besides light and warmth, the sun also sends out **UV rays**. It is our biggest source of UV. “Ultraviolet” means “beyond violet”: the rays lie right next to violet light, but are **invisible** to our eyes. Even so, they act on skin and eyes. A distinction is made between **UV-A**, **UV-B** and **UV-C**.

High up in the air lies the **ozone layer**. It swallows a large part of the dangerous UV radiation, and the dangerous UV-C almost completely. **Clouds** hold back only part of it. That is why you can get sunburn even on cloudy days. In the **mountains** the layer of air above us is thinner and holds back less. That is why the UV radiation is stronger there.

Too much UV radiation damages the skin. It turns red, hot and sore: **sunburn**. In the sun the skin makes more dark pigment, **melanin**. That is why it goes brown in summer. This tan protects a little, but not enough. Many sunburns raise the risk of skin cancer in the long run. The body does need some UV radiation, though, to make **vitamin D**.

UV rays can also irritate the **eyes** and damage them in the long run. Good **sunglasses** with UV protection help against this. **Clothes** protect best: at the beach it is better to keep a T-shirt on. Add to that a hat, sun cream and shade over midday. Wet skin does not protect against it.

UV radiation is also produced artificially. With **UV-C lamps** you can rid water and surfaces of germs. With UV light you check banknotes, whose security features then glow. UV radiation was discovered in **1801** by the German researcher **Johann Wilhelm Ritter**. He noticed that an invisible radiation acts beyond violet light.

gewusst: Bees can see UV light. Many flowers have patterns that are visible only in UV light and show the bees the way to the nectar.
Fresh snow throws back a large part of the UV radiation. That is why sun protection is especially important when skiing.

teile.einleitung: **Somatotropin** is the human growth hormone. In children and teenagers it makes bones and tissues grow. In adults, too, it has important tasks in metabolism.
wichtigste: Somatotropin is made in the anterior pituitary gland.
Many of its growth effects work through IGF-1 from the liver.
It is released in particularly large amounts during deep sleep.
It raises the blood sugar level.
Too much somatotropin leads to gigantism in children and to acromegaly in adults.
The hormone consists of 191 amino acids.

abschnitte.text: Somatotropin is made in the **pituitary gland**, more precisely in the **anterior pituitary**. The pituitary gland is a small gland on the underside of the brain. Special cells, the **somatotropic cells**, release the hormone into the blood. It is a **peptide hormone** made of **191 amino acids**. For comparison, insulin has only 51 amino acids.

Somatotropin often does not act directly but by a detour. It stimulates the **liver** to make the messenger substance **IGF-1**. That stands for insulin-like growth factor 1. IGF-1 promotes the growth of **bones** and tissues. As long as the **growth plates** in the bones are open, the bones can grow longer.

The largest release of growth hormone happens shortly after falling asleep. It takes place mainly during the **deep sleep phases**. Getting enough sleep is therefore important for growth. Somatotropin also influences metabolism. It acts as an **opponent of insulin** and **raises** the blood sugar level.

If the body makes too much somatotropin in childhood, the bones grow excessively long. This is called **giant growth** or gigantism. If the growth plates have already closed, the body no longer grows taller. Instead the hands, feet, chin and nose become larger. This disease is called **acromegaly**, and its most common cause is a benign tumour of the pituitary gland.

Children with too little growth hormone can be treated with somatotropin. In the past the hormone was obtained from the pituitary glands of people who had died. In some cases this transmitted the dangerous **Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease**. Today somatotropin is made by **genetic engineering**, in bacteria or cell cultures. This is much safer and provides enough hormone for everyone affected.

gewusst: The name somatotropin comes from Greek: soma means “body”.
Human growth hormone was one of the first medicines to be made with genetic engineering.

teile.einleitung: Addiction prevention means preventing addiction. It aims to stop people from becoming dependent in the first place. This is particularly important for children and teenagers.
wichtigste: Prevention means stopping something before it happens.
A typical feature of addiction is loss of control.
If the addictive substance is missing, withdrawal symptoms appear.
Gambling addiction is a behavioural addiction without a substance.
Self-confidence and good relationships protect against addiction.
Children and teenagers can get advice on the number 147.
The Federal Office of Public Health runs national prevention programmes.

abschnitte.text: The word **prevention** comes from the Latin “praevenire”, to come before. Addiction prevention aims to get ahead of addiction before it develops. It informs people about risks, strengthens children and teenagers and makes sure there are rules, such as age limits for selling alcohol and tobacco.

Anyone who is addicted can no longer decide for themselves how much they use or when they stop. Experts speak of **loss of control**. The body gets used to the addictive substance. If it is suddenly missing, **withdrawal symptoms** appear, such as restlessness, trembling or sleep problems. There are also **behavioural addictions** without a substance. In gambling addiction it is playing for money that makes people dependent.

People who believe in themselves, can solve problems and feel supported by others turn to addictive substances less often. Such **protective factors** are at the centre of addiction prevention. They include **self-confidence**, good friendships, hobbies and adults you can talk to.

**Peer pressure** arises when you want to belong and the others are joining in with something. It takes courage to say **no** anyway. Anyone who can do this protects themselves better against risky use. Real friends accept a no. It helps to think beforehand about what you want to say.

On the number **147**, **Pro Juventute** advises children and teenagers around the clock about all kinds of worries. For comparison: 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 144 the ambulance. At federal level the **Federal Office of Public Health** (FOPH) is responsible. It runs national strategies, for example on addiction, and works with the cantons and specialist bodies to do so.

gewusst: Advice on 147 is free and confidential, and you can also write via chat or message.
Many cantons have their own specialist offices for addiction prevention.

teile.einleitung: Theodor Kocher was a surgeon from Bern and one of the most famous doctors in Switzerland. He became known above all for his operations on the thyroid gland. In 1909 he became the first Swiss person to win the Nobel Prize.
wichtigste: Theodor Kocher lived from 1841 to 1917 and came from Bern.
From 1872 he headed the surgical clinic at the Inselspital in Bern.
He operated on thousands of people with goitre, an enlarged thyroid gland.
He cut the death rate in goitre operations to under one per cent.
In 1909 he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
The collar incision, the Kocher clamp and a manoeuvre for the shoulder are named after him.

abschnitte.text: Kocher studied medicine in Bern and trained further in several countries. At just 31 he became **professor of surgery** in Bern and headed the clinic at the **Inselspital**. He received offers from universities abroad, but stayed in Bern. There he worked until his death in 1917.

In Kocher's time very many people in Switzerland had a **goitre**. The reason was **iodine deficiency**: in the Alpine regions the soil and water contain little iodine. Without iodine the thyroid gland in the neck becomes enlarged. A large goitre can press on the windpipe and make breathing difficult. Kocher developed safe operations for such cases.

Kocher worked very precisely and took care over thorough **control of bleeding** and over **asepsis**, that is working free of germs. As a result the death rate in goitre operations fell from very high levels to **under one per cent**. For access he chose a crosswise **collar incision** in a fold of skin on the neck, the scar of which is hardly noticeable later.

Kocher observed that people whose whole thyroid gland had been removed later became sluggish, clumsy and mentally slowed. From this he realised that the **thyroid gland is vital**. After that he always left a remnant of the gland in place during operations. For his work on the thyroid gland he received the **Nobel Prize** in 1909.

Many things in medicine bear Kocher's name. The **Kocher clamp** is a clamp with toothed tips, used to grip tissue and blood vessels. It is still used today. With the **Kocher manoeuvre** a dislocated shoulder is put back into place by turning and guiding the arm in a fixed sequence.

gewusst: Kocher was the first surgeon in the world to receive a Nobel Prize.
In Bern, the Theodor Kocher Institute of the university commemorates him.

teile.einleitung: Umami is, besides sweet, sour, salty and bitter, one of the basic tastes. It describes a strong, savoury taste, as you know it from stock, Parmesan or soy sauce. The word comes from Japan.
wichtigste: Umami translated means roughly “delicious”.
The word comes from Japanese.
Kikunae Ikeda described umami in 1908.
The taste is mainly caused by glutamate.
Stock, Parmesan, soy sauce and ripe tomatoes taste strongly of umami.
