The Swiss spread Cenovis also tastes strongly of umami.

abschnitte.text: For a long time only four basic tastes were known: **sweet**, **sour**, **salty** and **bitter**. Today **umami** is counted as the fifth. The Japanese word means roughly **“delicious”** or “tasting good”. It describes a strong, spicy and savoury taste. On the tongue there are sensory cells that recognise exactly this taste.

The Japanese researcher **Kikunae Ikeda** described umami in **1908**. He asked himself why a soup made from **kombu seaweed** tastes so especially good. In doing so he found the substance responsible: **glutamate**. Shortly afterwards glutamate was made and sold as a seasoning. It took many more decades, however, before umami was recognised worldwide as a basic taste of its own.

**Glutamate** occurs naturally in many foods. Foods that are long-matured or cooked have especially much of it. **Stock** tastes savoury with umami. Long-matured cheese such as **Parmesan** does too. **Soy sauce** from Asia is made from soya beans, matured for a long time, and tastes salty and very umami. Ripe and dried **tomatoes** and mushrooms also have a lot of it. That is why they season sauces so well.

A Swiss example is **Cenovis**. This is a dark, savoury paste made from **brewer's yeast**, which you spread on bread and butter. **Yeast extract** tastes strongly of umami. A vegetable stock or a well-matured mountain cheese also bring a lot of umami to the table. Many cooks use such ingredients to make dishes taste rounder.

gewusst: Kikunae Ikeda founded, with a partner, a company that sold glutamate as a seasoning powder. It still exists today.
The riper tomatoes are, the more glutamate they contain.

teile.einleitung: **Skiing** is a popular winter sport in Switzerland. You glide down the mountain over the snow on two skis. Many children learn it early on at ski school.
wichtigste: When skiing, ski poles help with balance.
Ski goggles protect the eyes from wind, snow and light.
Beginners brake with the snowplough.
In Switzerland easy pistes are blue, medium ones red and difficult ones black.
You need sun cream in winter too.
The Lauberhorn race takes place in Wengen every year.

abschnitte.text: For skiing you need **skis**, ski boots and **ski poles**. The poles help with balance and with pushing off. You also use them when turning. **Ski goggles** fit closely around the eyes and protect against wind, snow and strong light. A **helmet** protects the head in a fall.

You get up the mountain comfortably with a **ski lift** or a chairlift. Then you ski down. Beginners first learn the **snowplough**. The tips of the skis point towards each other and the ends point apart. This slows you down and lets you stop.

In Switzerland the pistes are marked according to difficulty. **Blue** pistes are easy. **Red** pistes are of medium difficulty. **Black** pistes are difficult and steep. This way you can choose a run that suits your own ability.

You need **sun cream** in the mountains in winter too. Snow strongly reflects sunlight. In addition, the radiation is stronger at altitude than in the valley. That is why you quickly get **sunburnt**. Good ski goggles or sunglasses also protect the eyes.

In the **slalom** the gates are close together and you make many quick turns. In the **downhill**, by contrast, you race down the mountain at high speed. The **Lauberhorn race** in **Wengen** in the Bernese Oberland is one of the longest downhills in the World Cup and takes place every year in January. From 2022, **Marco Odermatt** from Nidwalden won the overall Alpine Skiing World Cup several times in a row. He is one of the best skiers in the world.

gewusst: The Lauberhorn race has been held since 1930 and is one of the oldest ski races in the world.
At the fastest points of the Lauberhorn, racers reach speeds of over 150 kilometres per hour.

teile.einleitung: A synapse is the point of contact where one nerve cell passes a signal on to the next cell. Most often this happens with chemical messenger substances that jump across a tiny gap. Our brain has an unimaginably large number of such connections, and they change constantly as we learn.
wichtigste: At a synapse, signals are passed from one nerve cell to the next.
Most often this happens through chemical messenger substances, the neurotransmitters.
Between the two cells lies a tiny gap, the synaptic cleft.
The brain has many trillions of synapses.
When we learn, synapses are strengthened or newly formed.
Some medicines and poisons act directly on the synapses.
The term synapse was coined around 1897 by the British researcher Charles Sherrington.

abschnitte.text: Nerve cells, also called **neurons**, pass on information as electrical signals. At the end of their long extension, the axon, they meet another cell. This point of contact is called a **synapse**. The other cell can be another nerve cell, a muscle cell or a gland cell. The word comes from Greek and means connection.

The two cells do not touch. Between them lies the **synaptic cleft**, much thinner than a hair. When an electrical signal arrives at the end of the first cell, it releases messenger substances from small sacs. These **neurotransmitters** travel across the gap. On the other side they dock onto matching **receptors** like a key in a lock. This creates a new electrical signal in the next cell.

There are many different neurotransmitters with different jobs. **Acetylcholine** gives muscles the command to contract. **Dopamine** plays a part in reward and motivation. Serotonin influences mood and sleep. Some messenger substances stimulate the next cell, others slow it down.

A human brain has around 86 billion nerve cells. Each of them can be connected to thousands of others through synapses. When we practise something, the synapses involved become stronger, which is called **synaptic plasticity**. Connections that are rarely used, on the other hand, are broken down. In this way the brain changes throughout life.

Many medicines act on the synapses, for example some drugs for depression or pain. Poisons also attack here. The arrow poison **curare** blocks the synapses between nerves and muscles, so that the muscles are paralysed. Caffeine and nicotine also affect signal transmission. In illnesses such as Parkinson's disease, there is too little of the messenger substance dopamine in certain parts of the brain.

begriffe.erklaerung: A nerve cell that passes on electrical signals.
A chemical messenger substance that carries signals across a synapse.
The tiny space between two cells at a synapse.
A docking point to which a matching messenger substance binds.

gewusst: Besides chemical synapses there are also electrical synapses, where the signal flows directly from cell to cell.
Toddlers have more synapses than adults, and unused ones are broken down later.
Transmission at a chemical synapse takes only about a thousandth of a second.

teile.einleitung: The tailbone is the very lowest part of the spine. It is small, lies above the bottom and consists of several vertebrae that have grown together. Researchers see it as the remains of a tail.
wichtigste: The tailbone lies at the lower end of the spine.
It consists of three to six small vertebrae, usually four.
Directly above it lies the **sacrum**.
It is roughly the shape of a small triangle with its point downwards.
The tailbone is considered the remains of a **tail**.
After falling on your bottom it often hurts.

abschnitte.text: The spine reaches from the head to the pelvis. Its lowest part is the **tailbone**. It consists of three to six small vertebrae, usually four. These have **fused** into a single bone. Directly above it lies the **sacrum**, which also consists of vertebrae that have grown together. The sacrum is firmly joined to the pelvis.

The tailbone is only a few centimetres long. It is much smaller than, for example, the pelvis. It gets narrower and narrower towards the bottom. That is why it looks roughly like a small **triangle** with its point downwards. Some **muscles** and **ligaments** are attached to the tailbone. They help to hold the organs in the lower abdomen in place.

abschnitte.titel: What is left of a tail
abschnitte.text: Many **vertebrates** have a tail at this point, for example dogs, cats or many monkeys. Apes and humans have no visible tail. In humans only the small tailbone is left of it. Researchers see this as a sign that our distant ancestors had a tail. A body part that has lost its earlier task is called a **remnant** or rudiment.

Anyone who falls on their bottom, for example on the ice or when sledging, can easily **bruise** their tailbone. This can hurt for some time, especially when sitting. A soft cushion can help then. A bruise usually heals by itself. If the pain lasts a long time, you have it examined by a doctor.

gewusst: The technical name of the tailbone, os coccygis, comes from the Greek word for cuckoo, because it resembles a cuckoo's beak.
In humans the vertebrae of the tailbone usually only fuse completely in the course of life.

teile.einleitung: Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can develop into different types of cell. Blood cells, skin cells or nerve cells, for example, come from them. This makes them something like the all-rounders among cells and a great hope for medicine.
wichtigste: Stem cells are not yet fixed to one task.
They can divide and form new stem cells as they do so.
They can develop into specialised cells such as blood or muscle cells.
A distinction is made between embryonic and adult stem cells.
In the bone marrow, stem cells constantly make new blood cells.
Stem cells can be used, for example, to treat leukaemia.
Research on embryonic stem cells is the subject of ethical debate.

abschnitte.text: Most cells in our body are **specialised**: a nerve cell carries signals, a red blood cell carries oxygen. Stem cells, on the other hand, are not yet fixed. They have two special abilities: they can divide again and again and form new stem cells as they do so. They can also **differentiate** into various cell types. This is how the many tissues of the body arise from them.

A human being develops from a single fertilised egg cell. In the first days it divides, and **embryonic stem cells** are formed. All the roughly 200 cell types of the body can develop from them. Experts call this **pluripotent**. That is exactly why they are particularly interesting for research.

Adults still have stem cells too, the **adult stem cells**. They are found, for example, in the bone marrow, in the skin or in the intestine. In the bone marrow they make billions of new blood cells every day. In the skin they replace dead cells. However, adult stem cells can only form certain types of cell.

The best-known use is **stem cell transplantation**. People with leukaemia, that is blood cancer, receive blood stem cells from a suitable donor. In Switzerland you can register as a donor with the foundation Blood Transfusion SRC Switzerland. Researchers hope one day to be able to repair damaged organs, nerves or heart muscle with stem cells. But many of these methods are still being tested.

Embryonic stem cells require early embryos to be used, which is why there is ethical debate about them. In Switzerland the **Stem Cell Research Act** has regulated what is allowed since 2005. In 2006 the Japanese researcher **Shin'ya Yamanaka** showed how normal body cells can be turned back into stem cells. These cells are called induced pluripotent stem cells. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2012.

begriffe.erklaerung: The development of a cell into a particular cell type.
Able to develop into almost all cell types of the body.
Tissue inside the bones in which blood stem cells are found.
The transfer of cells or organs from one person to another.

gewusst: The blood in a newborn baby's umbilical cord also contains many blood stem cells.
Plants have stem cells too, for example at the tips of shoots and roots.
Flatworms such as planarians can regrow a whole body from small pieces thanks to their many stem cells.

teile.einleitung: The skeletal muscles are all the muscles that are attached to our bones and move us. You need them for walking, jumping, laughing and even breathing. Humans have over 600 of these muscles, and we can control them at will.
wichtigste: You need your skeletal muscles to move.
Humans have over 600 skeletal muscles.
Skeletal muscles are attached to the bones by tendons.
A muscle can only pull, not push.
That is why muscles work in pairs as opponents.
Skeletal muscles can be controlled at will.
Training makes muscles stronger and gives them more stamina.

abschnitte.text: Skeletal muscles are the muscles that are connected to the skeleton. Under the microscope you can see fine cross stripes, which is why they are also called **striated muscle**. Unlike the heart muscle or the muscles in the intestine, we can move them consciously. In an adult they make up about 40 per cent of body weight. The largest muscle is the **gluteus maximus** in the buttocks.

A muscle consists of many bundles of **muscle fibres**. Each fibre is a long cell that can measure several centimetres. Inside the fibres there are tiny protein threads that can slide into each other. At its end the muscle turns into a strong **tendon**, which is firmly attached to the bone. The best known is the Achilles tendon at the heel.

The brain sends a command to the muscle along nerves. The muscle then contracts, becoming shorter and thicker. In doing so it pulls on the bone through the tendon and moves a joint. Because a muscle can only pull, it needs an **opponent**. In the arm the **biceps** bends the elbow and the **triceps** straightens it again.

When we laugh, many small muscles in the face work together. The **diaphragm** below the lungs is also a skeletal muscle and makes breathing possible. The calf muscles lift us onto our tiptoes when we walk. The back muscles keep us upright, even when we are just sitting. Even the eyes are turned by six small muscles.

Anyone who does sport regularly makes their muscles stronger and gives them more stamina. In **strength training** the muscle fibres become thicker. After great exertion you can get **sore muscles**, because tiny tears in the fibres have to heal. Muscles need protein from food, for example from dairy products, eggs or pulses. Breaks are important too, because the muscle is built up while you recover.

begriffe.erklaerung: A strong band that connects a muscle to the bone.
A muscle that reverses the movement of another muscle.
A long muscle cell that can contract.
Aching muscles after unusual exertion.

gewusst: The smallest skeletal muscle is the stapedius muscle in the middle ear.
Muscles produce a lot of heat when they work, which is why we get hot during sport.
When we are cold, the muscles shiver to warm the body.

teile.einleitung: Every person has to go to the toilet several times a day. In Switzerland it is mostly called the WC. If you know a few simple rules, you keep yourself and others healthy.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the toilet is mostly called the WC.
After using the WC you flush.
Only toilet paper belongs in the WC, not wet wipes.
After the WC you always wash your hands with soap.
Hand washing should take about 20 to 30 seconds.
The wastewater flows to the sewage treatment plant, the ARA.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland people mostly say **WC**. This comes from the English “water closet”. After using the toilet you press the **flush**. Then water flows through the bowl and washes everything into the **drain**. It is best to close the **lid** beforehand, so that less water splashes around.

abschnitte.titel: What may go in the WC
abschnitte.text: Only **toilet paper** belongs in the WC, because it dissolves in water. **Wet wipes**, cotton buds and other rubbish do not dissolve. They block the pipes and belong in the **rubbish bin**. This keeps the toilet clean and the pipes working.

After the WC you always wash your **hands with soap**. This removes germs that can make you ill. Rub your hands for about **20 to 30 seconds**, also between the fingers. That is about as long as singing a short song twice. Then you dry your hands with a **clean cloth**, because dry hands pass on fewer germs.

The wastewater from the WC flows through pipes to the **sewage treatment plant**. In Switzerland it is often called the **ARA**, short for “Abwasserreinigungsanlage”, which means wastewater treatment plant. There the water is cleaned in several steps. Only after that does it return to rivers and lakes.

gewusst: Anyone who often waits too long although they urgently need to go can get tummy ache. So it is best to go to the WC soon.
Almost every municipality in Switzerland is connected to a sewage treatment plant.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Samaritan Federation works to make sure that as many people as possible can give first aid. It offers courses, helps at events and supports blood donation drives. It is carried by many volunteers.
wichtigste: At the grassroots, the federation is organised in local Samaritan societies.
Before the learner driver’s permit for a car, you have to attend an emergency aid course.
The certificate may be at most 6 years old.
In the BLS-AED course you train chest compressions and defibrillation.
Many Samaritan societies organise blood donation drives with Blood Donation SRK.
The German surgeon Friedrich von Esmarch spread the Samaritan idea.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss Samaritan Federation** is the umbrella organisation of the **Samaritan societies**. At the grassroots it is organised in many **local societies**, which exist in villages and towns. The members mostly work **voluntarily**. They learn first aid, pass on their knowledge and provide medical cover, for example at sporting events, fairs or concerts. The Samaritan Federation is one of the rescue organisations of the **Swiss Red Cross**.

The name comes from a story in the Bible, the **Good Samaritan**. In it a man from Samaria helps an injured stranger by the wayside. In the 19th century the German surgeon **Friedrich von Esmarch** spread the Samaritan idea in the German-speaking world. He wanted laypeople to be able to help at accidents until a doctor arrives. Soon the first Samaritan societies also arose in Switzerland.

Anyone in Switzerland who wants to apply for the **learner driver’s permit** for a car must first have attended an **emergency aid course**. The certificate may be **at most 6 years** old when applying. Samaritan societies offer this course. There you learn to secure an accident scene, to raise the alarm, to position the injured correctly and to stop bleeding.

In the **BLS-AED course** you train **chest compressions** and the use of a **defibrillator**. A defibrillator gives the heart an electric shock when it is no longer beating properly. Such devices now hang at many railway stations and in sports halls. In addition, many Samaritan societies regularly organise **blood donation drives** in their municipality together with **Blood Donation SRK**.

gewusst: The abbreviation BLS comes from English and means “Basic Life Support”, that is, basic life-saving measures.
There are also Samaritan youth groups in which children and young people learn first aid.

teile.einleitung: Urine is the liquid with which the body gets rid of water and waste substances. It is made from the blood in the kidneys. From its colour and its ingredients you can tell a lot about health.
wichtigste: Urine consists of about 95 per cent water.
The most important dissolved waste substance is urea.
An adult passes about 1.5 litres of urine a day.
Very dark urine often shows that you are not drinking enough.
Sugar in the urine can point to diabetes.
In doping controls the urine is often examined.

abschnitte.text: Urine consists of about **95 per cent water**. Dissolved in it are **salts** and various **breakdown substances**. The most important dissolved waste substance is **urea**. It is formed when the body breaks down proteins. A healthy adult passes roughly **1.5 litres** of urine a day. The amount depends greatly on how much you drink and sweat.

The two **kidneys** constantly filter the blood. First a great deal of **primary urine** is formed, in an adult far more than a hundred litres a day. Then the kidneys take most of the water and important nutrients back into the blood. What is left is the much smaller amount of **final urine**. It flows through the **ureters** into the **bladder**, where it is collected until you go to the toilet.

Normal urine is pale yellow. If you drink little, the kidneys save water, and the urine becomes **more concentrated and darker**. A very dark yellow urine therefore often shows that you have **not drunk enough**. A pale yellow urine usually shows that you are drinking enough. Some foods, such as beetroot, can also change the colour for a short time.

abschnitte.titel: Urine as a clue to illnesses
abschnitte.text: Normally the kidneys take all the **sugar** back into the blood. If the blood sugar is too high, as in **diabetes**, they cannot manage this, and sugar gets into the urine. With a **test strip**, a doctor can quickly check the urine. Its small fields change colour with sugar, blood or protein. In this way you get first clues about illnesses in a short time.

In top-level sport, the urine is often examined in a **doping control**. Many banned substances and their breakdown products can be detected in it. Athletes give a **urine sample** under supervision for this. In Switzerland the foundation **Swiss Sport Integrity** is responsible.

gewusst: In the past doctors even tested urine with the tongue: if it tasted sweet, that was a clue to diabetes. That is where the name “diabetes mellitus” comes from, and mellitus means “honey-sweet”.
The yellow colour of urine comes from a pigment that is formed when blood pigment is broken down.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss food pyramid shows at a glance how to eat a balanced diet. It comes from the Swiss Society for Nutrition and the federal government. The higher up something stands, the less of it you should eat.
wichtigste: The pyramid is published by the Swiss Society for Nutrition together with the federal government.
The higher the level, the smaller the recommended amount.
The broad base is made up of unsweetened drinks.
One portion of vegetables is about 120 g.
On the level of starchy side dishes stand cereals, potatoes and pulses, best as wholegrain.
Recommended daily are 3 portions of milk and dairy products.
With that goes a small portion of unsalted nuts each day.

abschnitte.text: The **food pyramid** is divided into several levels. At the bottom it is wide, at the top pointed. This shows a simple principle: **the higher the level, the smaller the recommended amount**. It is published by the **Swiss Society for Nutrition** together with the federal government. No food is forbidden, what matters is the amount and the variety.

Right at the bottom, on the widest level, stand **unsweetened drinks**. These include water, mineral water and unsweetened tea. Adults should drink about 1 to 2 litres of them daily. In sport or heat you need more. Sugary drinks do not belong here but right at the top.

abschnitte.titel: Vegetables, fruit and starchy side dishes
abschnitte.text: On the next level follow **vegetables and fruit**. Recommended are five portions a day in different colours, of which three portions are vegetables and two portions fruit. One portion corresponds to **about 120 g**, roughly a handful. Above it lies the level of **starchy side dishes**: cereals such as bread, pasta and rice, plus **potatoes** and **pulses** such as lentils. Here the pyramid recommends mainly **wholegrain products**, because they contain more fibre.

Further up stand **milk and dairy products** with **3 portions** a day, for example a glass of milk, a yoghurt and a piece of cheese. Added to this is one portion of other **protein sources** such as meat, fish, eggs or tofu. The next level belongs to **oils, fats and nuts**. Recommended are high-quality vegetable oils in small amounts and a small portion of **unsalted nuts** each day.

Right at the top, in the tip, stand **sweets**, salty snacks and sugary drinks. You may enjoy them, but only **in small amounts**. The pyramid adds to these rules with hints about enough **exercise** in everyday life. Anyone who keeps to the levels usually gets all the important nutrients without having to count calories.

gewusst: Similar food pyramids exist in many countries, but each is built a little differently.
Pulses such as lentils and chickpeas supply both starch and a lot of protein.

teile.einleitung: Thrombin is an enzyme in the blood and plays the main role in blood clotting. It makes sure that a dissolved protein turns into solid threads that close a wound. At the same time the body has brakes so that thrombin does not act too strongly.
wichtigste: Thrombin splits fibrinogen into fibrin, which forms solid threads.
Thrombin is made from the inactive precursor prothrombin, also called factor II.
It belongs to the serine proteases, that is, protein-splitting enzymes.
Antithrombin inhibits thrombin, and heparin strongly boosts this inhibition.
Hirudin from the saliva of the leech inhibits thrombin directly.
Dabigatran is a medicine that blocks thrombin directly.

abschnitte.text: Dissolved **fibrinogen** floats in the blood. When there is an injury, **thrombin** splits small pieces off it. The building blocks that are left join up into long **fibrin threads**. These form a net in which platelets and blood cells get caught. This makes a solid plug that closes the wound.

Thrombin is not constantly active in the blood. It is made in the liver as the precursor **prothrombin** (factor II), and for this the liver needs **vitamin K**. When there is an injury, a complex of the factors Xa and Va splits prothrombin into thrombin (factor IIa). Thrombin is a **serine protease**: it has a serine in its active centre and cuts other proteins.

Thrombin activates, among others, the factors **V**, **VIII** and **XI**. These in turn help to make more thrombin. Such **positive feedback** makes sure that clotting gets going quickly. In addition, thrombin activates the **platelets** so that they stick together.

So that the blood does not clot everywhere, there are opponents. **Antithrombin** binds thrombin and factor Xa, and the medicine **heparin** speeds up this inhibition many times over. On the cells of the vessel wall sits **thrombomodulin**. Bound to it, thrombin activates **protein C**, which breaks down the factors Va and VIIIa and so slows clotting.

With its saliva the leech releases **hirudin** into the wound, a strong direct thrombin inhibitor. Modelled on it, medicines such as **bivalirudin** were developed. **Dabigatran** is a tablet that blocks thrombin directly. Such drugs help to prevent blood clots in people at increased risk.

gewusst: One and the same thrombin can promote or slow clotting, depending on whether it is bound to thrombomodulin.
Leeches are still sometimes used in medicine today because of their hirudin.

teile.einleitung: The vocal folds are two fine folds of tissue in the larynx. When air flows between them, they vibrate and produce the sound of our voice. In everyday language they are often also called vocal cords.
wichtigste: The vocal folds lie in the **larynx**.
The gap between them is called the **glottis**.
The voice is normally produced when **breathing out**.
Vocal folds that are stretched more tightly vibrate faster and give a higher note.
Longer and thicker vocal folds sound deeper, which is why men usually have deeper voices.
When breathing calmly, the vocal folds are wide open.
Constant overuse can cause **singer's nodules**.

abschnitte.text: The vocal folds are stretched inside the **larynx** between its cartilages. The larynx sits at the front of the neck, on top of the windpipe. That is why it is also called the **voice box**. The two vocal folds border a gap on the left and right, the **glottis**. The air we breathe flows through it. When we breathe calmly, the glottis is wide open so that the air can flow freely.

To speak, the vocal folds are brought close together until they are almost closed. When **breathing out**, the air presses against them and makes them **vibrate**. This produces the sound. How fast they vibrate is measured in **hertz**: one hertz is one vibration per second. If someone sings a note of 220 hertz, the vocal folds vibrate 220 times a second. The mouth, throat and nose then shape the sound into speech sounds and words.

When the vocal folds are **stretched more tightly**, they vibrate faster and the note gets higher. More loosely stretched vocal folds give lower notes. Size also plays a part: **longer and thicker** vocal folds vibrate more slowly. This is similar to a thick guitar string. Men usually have longer vocal folds than women and so a deeper voice. When teenagers grow, the larynx grows too and the voice gets deeper, and this is called the **breaking of the voice**.

Anyone who often uses their voice too loudly or wrongly irritates the vocal folds. Small thickenings can form there, called **singer's nodules**. They make the voice hoarse. People who speak or sing a lot, such as teachers, are often affected. Breaks, drinking enough and a good speaking technique help against overuse. If **hoarseness** lasts a long time, you have the larynx examined by a doctor.

gewusst: When singing high notes, the vocal folds can vibrate many hundreds of times a second.
When whispering, the vocal folds do not vibrate, and the sounds are made only by the air flowing past.

teile.einleitung: Addiction Switzerland, in German “Sucht Schweiz”, is a foundation that deals with questions about addiction. It carries out research, provides information and works for prevention, that is for stopping addiction from developing in the first place.
wichtigste: Addiction Switzerland is a non-profit, independent foundation.
It is based in Lausanne in the canton of Vaud.
In French it is called “Addiction Suisse”.
Its tasks are prevention, research and information.
It deals with alcohol, tobacco, cannabis and gambling.
In Switzerland it carries out the HBSC pupil survey.

abschnitte.text: **Addiction Switzerland** is a non-profit and independent **foundation**. It is based in **Lausanne** in the canton of Vaud. From there it works for the whole of Switzerland and in several national languages. In French it is called “Addiction Suisse”. It used to be called the **Swiss Institute for the Prevention of Alcohol and Drug Problems**, SFA for short. The new name shows that it deals with all forms of addiction.

The foundation develops **prevention projects**, for example teaching materials for schools. It **researches** how much and why people use addictive substances. And it **informs** professionals, parents and young people with leaflets and websites. Punishment and police work are not among its tasks. The authorities are responsible for those.

Addiction Switzerland deals with addictive substances such as **alcohol**, **tobacco** and **cannabis**. There are also medicines that can be addictive. **Behavioural addictions**, in which no substance is taken, are also included. Examples are gambling and excessive use of the internet and games.

The **HBSC study** stands for “Health Behaviour in School-aged Children”. It runs in many countries under the umbrella of the **World Health Organization, WHO**. In Switzerland Addiction Switzerland regularly surveys pupils aged 11 to 15 for it. This shows how young people are doing and what changes over time.

gewusst: Thanks to the HBSC study, Swiss young people can be compared with people of the same age in many other countries.
Addiction Switzerland works in German, French and Italian.

teile.einleitung: People who eat a vegan diet eat no products from animals. Besides meat and fish, milk, eggs and honey are also left out. With good planning you can eat a balanced diet this way, but some nutrients need special attention.
wichtigste: Vegans avoid all animal products, including milk, eggs and honey.
Tofu is made from soya beans.
Seitan consists mainly of wheat protein.
You should take vitamin B12 as a supplement.
Many gummy bears contain gelatine and are not vegan.
The word “vegan” was coined by Donald Watson in 1944.

abschnitte.text: **Vegetarians** eat no meat and no fish. **Vegans** go further: they leave out all products from animals, so also **milk**, **eggs** and **honey**. Sometimes animal ingredients are hidden in foods. Many **gummy bears** are not vegan, because they contain **gelatine**. Gelatine is obtained from the skin and bones of animals. Vegan gummy bears use plant-based gelling agents.

The word “vegan” was coined by the Englishman **Donald Watson** in **1944**. In the same year he founded the **Vegan Society**. He formed the word from the first and last letters of the English word “vegetarian”. People eat a vegan diet for different reasons, for example because of animals, the environment or health. Others consciously also eat animal products. Both are personal decisions.

Many vegans eat substitutes for meat. **Tofu** is made from **soya beans**. First a soya milk is made from them, which is then made to curdle, similar to cheese making. **Seitan** consists mainly of **wheat protein**, the sticky protein **gluten**. For people with coeliac disease, who cannot tolerate gluten, seitan is therefore unsuitable. Lentils, beans and chickpeas also provide a lot of protein.

Plant foods provide practically no usable **vitamin B12**. Specialist bodies therefore recommend vegans a **supplement** or fortified foods. **Omega-3 fatty acids**, which otherwise often come from fish, are found in **linseed**, linseed oil, walnuts and algae oil. **Calcium** is provided by kale, broccoli, almonds and fortified plant drinks. Children and teenagers in particular should plan a vegan diet with a professional.

gewusst: Every year on 1 November it is World Vegan Day.
The name tofu comes from Chinese, where tofu has been eaten for many centuries.

teile.einleitung: Thyroxine is the most important hormone of the thyroid gland. It controls how fast the metabolism works throughout the body. To make it, the body needs iodine, which we take in with our food.
wichtigste: Thyroxine is called T4 for short, because it contains four iodine atoms.
In the tissues it is mostly converted into the more active triiodothyronine (T3).
Thyroxine raises the basal metabolic rate and heat production.
In the thyroid gland it is stored on the protein thyroglobulin.
With iodine deficiency the thyroid gland grows into a goitre.
In Switzerland iodised table salt has existed since 1922.

abschnitte.text: The **thyroid gland** sits at the front of the neck and is shaped like a butterfly. It makes the hormones **thyroxine (T4)** and **triiodothyronine (T3)**. The number in the abbreviation shows how many iodine atoms are in the molecule. The hormones are made on a large protein, **thyroglobulin**, and are stored in the colloid of the thyroid follicles. When needed they are split off and released into the blood.

In the cells, thyroxine is mostly converted into **T3** by splitting off an iodine atom, which is the biologically more active form. Thyroid hormones **raise the basal metabolic rate**: the cells use more energy and produce more heat. They are also indispensable for the **growth** and maturing of the brain. That is why all newborns are tested for a deficiency.

The **pituitary gland** releases the hormone **TSH**, which drives the thyroid gland. If there is enough thyroxine in the blood, less TSH is made. With **iodine deficiency** too little thyroxine is made, the brake falls away, and TSH rises. TSH makes the thyroid gland grow, and a **goitre** (struma) develops.

With an **underactive thyroid**, people feel tired, feel the cold easily and often put on weight. They then take **levothyroxine** every day, which is T4 made artificially. With an **overactive thyroid** the body works too fast: a racing heart, sweating and weight loss are typical. A common cause is **Graves' disease**, in which antibodies permanently activate the TSH receptor.

In the past, very many people in Switzerland had a goitre, because the soil and water in the Alps contain little iodine. In **1922** Switzerland was one of the first countries to introduce **iodised table salt**. Goitre and severe developmental disorders caused by iodine deficiency fell sharply afterwards. To this day, iodised salt is a matter of course in many Swiss kitchens.

gewusst: Levothyroxine is among the most frequently taken medicines of all.
Almost all the iodine in the body is used to make the thyroid hormones.

teile.einleitung: The triceps is a strong muscle on the back of the upper arm. It makes sure that you can straighten your arm at the elbow, for example when throwing or when pushing yourself up from a press-up.
wichtigste: The triceps lies at the back of the upper arm.
It straightens the arm at the elbow joint.
The muscle has three heads, hence the name “tri” for three.
Its opposing muscle is the biceps, which bends the arm.
The tendon of the triceps attaches at the olecranon of the ulna.
It is controlled by the radial nerve.

abschnitte.text: In technical language the triceps is called the **musculus triceps brachii**, that is the three-headed muscle of the upper arm. It covers almost the whole back of the upper arm. If you straighten your arm and grip the back of the upper arm with the other hand, you feel it go hard. The triceps is a large muscle and makes up a significant part of the muscles of the upper arm.

A muscle head is a start of a muscle on a bone. The triceps has three of them: a **long head**, a **lateral head** and a **medial head**. The long head begins at the shoulder blade, the other two at the upper arm bone. Because the long head runs across the shoulder and the elbow, it acts on two joints. At the bottom all three heads join into one common tendon.

The tendon of the triceps runs to the **olecranon** of the ulna. This is the tip of bone that you feel when your arm is bent. When the triceps contracts, the forearm is pulled backwards and the arm is straightened. A muscle can only pull, not push. That is why every movement needs a muscle that pulls in the other direction.

The **biceps** lies at the front of the upper arm and bends the elbow. The triceps does the opposite and straightens it. Such pairs are called **opposing muscles**. When one muscle works, the other relaxes. The triceps is controlled by the **radial nerve**. This nerve supplies the extensor muscles at the back of the arm.

You need the triceps whenever you push yourself up with your arms or push something away. In a **press-up** it does a large part of the work when you push up. It also works when you push yourself up from sitting, when you throw a ball or when you swim. In gymnastics you need it for the handstand and on the parallel bars.

gewusst: The name triceps comes from Latin: “tri” means three and “caput” means head.
The triceps is bigger than the biceps, although people usually talk about the biceps when it comes to strong arms.

teile.einleitung: Trans fatty acids are special unsaturated fatty acids. In the past they arose mainly in the industrial hardening of vegetable oils. Because they harm the heart, they are strictly limited in Switzerland and many other countries.
wichtigste: In trans fatty acids the double bond is in the trans form, in natural fatty acids mostly in the cis form.
Large amounts arose in partial fat hardening.
Trans fatty acids raise LDL cholesterol and lower HDL cholesterol.
In Switzerland a maximum of 2 grams per 100 grams of fat has applied since 2008.
Denmark was the first country to introduce a limit, in 2003.
In the milk and meat of ruminants they occur naturally in small amounts.

abschnitte.text: Unsaturated fatty acids have at least one **double bond** in their chain. In natural fats it is mostly in the **cis form**: the hydrogen atoms sit on the same side, and the chain has a kink. In the **trans form** they sit opposite each other, and the chain stays **straight**. As a result trans fatty acids behave more like solid fats.

To make liquid vegetable oils spreadable and long-lasting, they were **hardened**. In **partial fat hardening** (partial hydrogenation), some double bonds are not saturated but rearranged. This is how trans fatty acids are formed. Such fats used to be found in **frying oils**, **puff pastry**, biscuits and margarines.

Trans fatty acids **raise** the unfavourable **LDL cholesterol** and **lower** the favourable **HDL cholesterol**. So they worsen the balance twice over. This raises the risk of hardening of the arteries and **heart attack**. That is why experts advise eating as few industrially produced trans fatty acids as possible.

**Denmark** limited industrial trans fatty acids in **2003**, the first country to do so. **Switzerland** followed in **2008**: since then, vegetable oils and fats may contain at most **2 grams** of trans fatty acids per 100 grams of fat. The World Health Organization (**WHO**) calls on all countries to ban industrially produced trans fatty acids from food. Many manufacturers have meanwhile changed their recipes.

It is not possible to do entirely without trans fatty acids. **Bacteria in the rumen** of cows, sheep and goats make them in small amounts. That is why **butter**, milk and beef contain small shares. These natural amounts are much smaller than those that used to be in hardened industrial fats.

gewusst: Margarine was long considered a healthier alternative to butter, but used to contain a lot of trans fatty acids.
Today fats are mostly fully hardened or processed in other ways, which produces hardly any trans fatty acids.

teile.einleitung: Pride is a feeling we have when we have managed something difficult. We are pleased with ourselves and often show it with an upright posture. But too much pride can also become a problem.
wichtigste: You feel pride when you have managed something difficult.
Proud people stand **upright with their head held high**.
The opposite of pride is **shame**.
In German people say “proud as a **peacock**” and “proud as **Oskar**”.
Exaggerated pride in which you look down on others is called **arrogance**.
You can rightly be proud when you have learnt something through practice.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who masters a difficult task is pleased with themselves. This feeling is called **pride**. It comes, for example, when you ride a bike without stabilisers for the first time or pass a hard exam. Pride is best when you have **practised hard** and then it works. You can also be proud of other people, for example of a friend who has achieved something great. Parents then often say: “I'm proud of you!”

Feelings also show in the body. Proud people straighten up, raise their **chin** and push their chest out a little. They often smile as they do so. This posture is recognised all over the world. With **shame**, the opposite of pride, it is the other way round: you lower your head, make yourself small and would most like to hide.

The **peacock** spreads a magnificent fan with its colourful feathers. That is why people say of someone who shows off: “proud as a peacock”. The German saying **“stolz wie Oskar”**, meaning “proud as Oskar”, describes someone who is very proud. Where the name Oskar comes from is not clearly known. A well-known proverb goes: “Pride comes before a fall.” It warns against becoming too arrogant.

Healthy pride strengthens **self-confidence**. Anyone who knows they can do something also dares to try new things. But if pride is exaggerated, you think you are better than others. This is called **arrogance** or conceit. Arrogant people look down on others and do not listen well. Anyone who is happy about other people's successes and praises them, on the other hand, shows real greatness.

gewusst: Even small children show pride, for example when they proudly show their parents a picture they have painted themselves.
Even people who have been blind from birth show the typical upright winner's posture when they succeed.
